details.name: Rubber moulded ball
details.description: A rubber moulded ball has its panels moulded into a single rubber shell rather than stitched, which makes it the toughest and most weatherproof type at this budget. It shrugs off concrete, gravel, wet ground and school-playground abuse that would quickly wear out softer balls, and it needs no care beyond a rinse. The trade-off is a harder, less cushioned touch. Choose a size 5 moulded ball with a butyl bladder for adult and teen practice on rough Indian grounds where one ball has to survive daily use.

details.name: Machine-stitched PVC ball
details.description: A machine-stitched PVC ball is the classic step up from a moulded ball: a PVC outer cover stitched into panels over a bladder, giving a softer touch and truer flight for passing and shooting practice. It plays best on grass and artificial turf; on harsh concrete the stitching and cover wear faster. Look for a 32-panel design, a butyl bladder for better air retention, and even stitching with no loose threads. This is the right category for casual grass games, school teams and regular training on decent surfaces.

details.description: A small training ball usually means a size 3 ball — the size recommended for children roughly between six and ten years — or a mini skills ball used for close-control drills. The smaller circumference forces quicker feet, tighter touches and better ball mastery, which is why coaches use small balls for dribbling and juggling practice even with older beginners. For young children it is also simply the correct, safer size to learn with. Pick a machine-stitched PVC size 3 with a bladder that holds air well, in a bright colour that is easy to spot.

Vi is an all-India integrated GSM operator providing mobile telephony, wireless broadband and internet services to prepaid and postpaid customers, including bundled entertainment and gaming offers alongside its recharge and postpaid plans. Siemens' association with India dates to the London–Calcutta telegraph line of 1870, and it set up its first Mumbai manufacturing workshop in the 1950s. In India the company now operates through three businesses — Digital Industries, Smart Infrastructure and Mobility — following the demerger of its energy business into Siemens Energy India. Its work covers industrial automation and digitalisation software, building and power-distribution technology, and rail and metro systems including signalling, electrification and rolling-stock components, with manufacturing and sales sites including Kalwa, Pune, Vadodara, Gurugram and Chennai.
details.modelTitle: Incorporated 1957 · Mumbai

details.name: ABB India
details.description: ABB India Limited is the Indian arm of the Swedish-Swiss ABB group, incorporated in 1949, with its registered office at Peenya, Bengaluru. Its predecessor companies ASEA of Sweden and Brown Boveri of Switzerland had a presence in India for over a century before that. ABB India works in electrification, automation and digitalisation: its products include switchgear and vacuum circuit breakers, motors, generators and drives, EV-charging infrastructure, industrial robotics, control-room solutions and measurement and analytics. It serves utilities, industry, infrastructure and transport, including automotive, buildings, cement, chemicals, data centres, mining and ports. Manufacturing sites include Faridabad, Vadodara, Nashik, and the Bengaluru campuses at Peenya and Nelamangala.
details.modelTitle: Incorporated 1949 · Bengaluru

details.name: Schneider Electric India
details.description: Schneider Electric India Private Limited, incorporated on 24 February 1995 with its registered office in New Delhi, is the Indian company of Schneider Electric, the French group whose history dates to 1836. In December 2025 it inaugurated a new corporate campus at DLF Downtown, Gurugram. The company describes India as its largest employee base globally and a hub for talent, innovation, research and development and manufacturing. Its India business covers energy management and industrial automation: electrical distribution equipment, building and home automation, data-centre power and cooling, industrial control products, and digital services and software for buildings, factories, infrastructure and electricity grids.
details.modelTitle: Incorporated 1995 · New Delhi

details.name: CG Power
details.description: CG Power and Industrial Solutions Limited is headquartered at CG House, Worli, Mumbai. It was incorporated on 28 April 1937 as Crompton Greaves Limited and changed its name to CG Power and Industrial Solutions Limited with effect from 27 February 2017; it is now part of the Murugappa Group through Tube Investments of India. The company provides end-to-end solutions for the management and application of electrical energy, organised in two segments. Power Systems makes transformers, switchgear and circuit breakers and undertakes substation and transmission-and-distribution projects. Industrial Systems makes low- and medium-voltage motors, generators and drives, and supplies traction machines, propulsion systems and signalling products to Indian Railways.
details.modelTitle: Incorporated 1937 · Mumbai

details.name: Polycab India
details.description: Polycab India Limited was incorporated as Polycab Wires Private Limited on 10 January 1996 in Mumbai, where it is headquartered, and took its present name in 2018. It manufactures wires and cables for sectors including energy and power grids, building and mobility infrastructure, manufacturing and exploration, and has expanded into fast-moving electrical goods: fans, switches, switchgear, water heaters, solar products, conduits and accessories, home automation solutions and luminaires for residential, commercial and industrial applications. Fortune India records 28 manufacturing facilities, two of them joint ventures, across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Uttarakhand and Daman and Diu, and a presence in more than 70 countries.
details.modelTitle: Incorporated 1996 · Mumbai

details.name: Legrand India
details.description: Legrand India is the Indian business of Legrand, the French specialist in electrical and digital building infrastructure based in Limoges. It entered India in 1996, setting up its head office in Mumbai, followed by factories, plants and sales offices across the country, and later a global R&D centre at Sinnar, Nashik. Its India range covers energy distribution, wiring devices, home automation, structured cabling, lighting management solutions, cable management and industrial application products, including miniature circuit breakers, residual-current devices and distribution boards. A company press release describes seven manufacturing units, three R&D centres and 28 offices in India, sold through distribution partners and retail outlets nationwide.

title: Punjabi Motivational Shayari on Life: Original Lines with Meaning
summary: Original Punjabi motivational couplets in Gurmukhi with simple English meanings for captions, reflection, and encouragement.
editorial: These verses were written for VisitBest's refreshed page and are not copied from songs or published poems.
items: ਰਾਹ ਔਖਾ ਹੋਵੇ ਤਾਂ ਹੌਸਲਾ ਹੋਰ ਪੱਕਾ ਕਰ, ਮੰਜ਼ਿਲ ਦੂਰ ਨਹੀਂ ਜੇ ਕਦਮ ਸੱਚਾ ਕਰ।

Rising after a fall defines life; every morning opens a new sky.
ਛੋਟੇ ਕਦਮਾਂ ਨਾਲ ਵੱਡੇ ਸੁਪਨੇ ਸਜਦੇ, ਮਿਹਨਤ ਵਾਲੇ ਹੱਥ ਕਦੇ ਖਾਲੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਰਹਿੰਦੇ।
Big dreams grow from small steps; hardworking hands do not remain empty.
ਆਪਣੀ ਰੌਸ਼ਨੀ ਨੂੰ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਦੇ ਡਰ ਨਾਲ ਨਾ ਢੱਕ, ਸੱਚੇ ਦਿਲ ਨਾਲ ਤੁਰ ਤੇ ਆਪਣੀ ਮੰਜ਼ਿਲ ਲੱਭ।
Do not hide your light because of others' fear; move sincerely toward your goal.
ਵੇਲਾ ਬਦਲਦਾ ਰਹਿੰਦਾ, ਤੂੰ ਨੀਅਤ ਸਾਫ਼ ਰੱਖ, ਅੱਜ ਬੀਜ ਮਿਹਨਤ ਦਾ, ਕੱਲ੍ਹ ਫਲ ਆਪਣੇ ਹੱਥ।
Time keeps changing; keep your intent clear and today's effort will bear fruit.

title: Punjabi Sad Shayari: Original Reflective Lines with Meaning
summary: Original Punjabi lines about distance, memory, and healing, presented in Gurmukhi with simple English meanings.
editorial: These lines are newly written for VisitBest. They avoid copied lyrics and are intended for personal reflection, not to romanticise prolonged distress.
items: ਚੁੱਪ ਰਹਿ ਕੇ ਵੀ ਦਿਲ ਕਿੰਨੀ ਗੱਲ ਸੁਣਾਉਂਦਾ, ਤੇਰਾ ਨਾਮ ਆਵੇ ਤਾਂ ਸਮਾਂ ਰੁਕ ਜਾਂਦਾ।
Even in silence the heart tells many stories; time seems to pause when your name appears.
ਰਾਹ ਵੱਖ ਹੋ ਗਏ, ਯਾਦਾਂ ਦਾ ਸ਼ਹਿਰ ਨਾ ਬਦਲਿਆ, ਦਿਨ ਤਾਂ ਲੰਘ ਗਿਆ ਪਰ ਦਿਲ ਦਾ ਪਹਿਰ ਨਾ ਬਦਲਿਆ।
Our roads separated, but the city of memories did not change.
ਮੀਂਹ ਨੇ ਖਿੜਕੀ ਉੱਤੇ ਪੁਰਾਣੀ ਗੱਲ ਲਿਖੀ, ਮੈਂ ਹੱਸ ਕੇ ਮਿਟਾਈ ਪਰ ਅੱਖ ਫਿਰ ਵੀ ਭਿੱਜੀ।
Rain wrote an old story on the window; I erased it smiling, yet my eyes were wet.
ਕੁਝ ਰਿਸ਼ਤੇ ਮੁੱਕ ਕੇ ਵੀ ਅੰਦਰ ਚੱਲਦੇ ਰਹਿੰਦੇ, ਅਸੀਂ ਅੱਗੇ ਵਧਦੇ ਹਾਂ, ਸਾਏ ਪਿੱਛੇ ਰਹਿੰਦੇ।
Some relationships continue inside us after ending; we move ahead while shadows remain.
ਦਰਦ ਨੂੰ ਸ਼ਬਦ ਮਿਲੇ ਤਾਂ ਸਾਹ ਹੌਲਾ ਹੋਇਆ, ਰਾਤ ਲੰਮੀ ਸੀ ਪਰ ਸਵੇਰ ਦਾ ਰਾਹ ਖੁਲਿਆ।
When pain found words, breathing became easier; the long night still opened toward morning.

details.name: Birla White WallCare
details.description: Birla White WallCare Putty is India's best-known white-cement putty, made by UltraTech's Birla White unit and sold through a very wide stockist network. It is a water-resistant base coat with extra hydrophobic polymers, positioned on superior whiteness, strong bonding and a smooth, bright finish for interior and exterior plaster and concrete. It suits homeowners, painters and contractors who want a dependable branded base under premium paints. Always verify the exact variant — WallCare, Excel, WallSeal or Levelling MF — plus pack size, manufacturing date and the surface-preparation and curing instructions for that variant.

details.description: JK wall putty is sold under two related JK houses in India: JK Cement's WallMaxX range, including WallMaxX Advanced and Professional, and JK Lakshmi Cement's JK Lakshmiplast Smart Wall Putty. Both are white-cement, polymer-enriched powders for interior and exterior plaster and concrete, positioned on whiteness, smoothness, adhesion and resistance to flaking. They suit contractors, painters and homeowners working through dealer networks, especially in north and central India. Verify which JK company, which MaxX or Smart variant, pack size and batch you are actually buying, because listings often mix the two ranges.

It suits homeowners and painters already using Asian Paints primers and paints who want system compatibility. Verify the SmartCare variant, pack size, whether a Damp Sheath or primer layer is required, and all curing instructions.

It suits homeowners, painters and contractors buying through Berger dealers who want the putty, primer and paint from one system. Verify the exact Bison variant, interior or exterior use, pack size, batch freshness and Berger's surface-preparation sequence.

Nerolac describes this putty for interior and exterior concrete and mortar, with waterproofing, resistance to dampness and efflorescence, easy sanding with less dusting, and a smooth white finish where a separate wall primer can be avoided. details.name: Microsoft
details.description: Microsoft has had a presence in India since 1990, when it set up its first office in Hyderabad. Its main research and engineering arm in the country, the Microsoft India Development Center (IDC), was set up in Hyderabad in 1998 and now also works from Bengaluru and Noida. Microsoft describes IDC as one of its largest R&D centres outside its Redmond headquarters. IDC teams contribute to products and services including Azure, Windows, Office and Bing. In India, Microsoft sells and supports its cloud, software and devices portfolio for businesses, government and consumers, working with the Indian government, the IT industry, academia and the local developer community.

details.name: Google
details.description: Google began its India operations in 2004, opening an engineering research and development centre in Bengaluru and planning a customer support centre in Hyderabad. Contemporary reports described the Bengaluru centre as Google's first full-fledged engineering facility outside the United States, working on data mining, data warehousing, business intelligence and knowledge management. Google India has since maintained offices in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Gurugram and Mumbai. Its Indian teams support engineering, product development, sales and customer operations for Google products used in India, including Search, YouTube, Android and Google Cloud, while the Hyderabad and Bengaluru offices remain its principal engineering locations in the country.

details.name: Amazon
details.description: Amazon entered India first through Junglee.com, a shopping comparison site launched in February 2012, and then launched its marketplace, Amazon.in, in June 2013, initially selling books and films and television shows. Its first fulfilment centre was set up near Mumbai, and a second opened in Bengaluru in January 2014. Amazon also runs development centres in Bengaluru, Chennai and Hyderabad that build software and applications supporting Amazon's websites worldwide, including web services, search and digital products. Today Amazon India operates the Amazon.in marketplace, Amazon Web Services and Prime services in India, with fulfilment and delivery infrastructure across the country.

details.description: IBM has been present in India since 1992, when it re-entered the market after an earlier exit in the 1970s, initially through a joint venture with the Tata Group. Its regional headquarters are in Bengaluru, with offices in cities including New Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai. IBM India combines consulting, technology services, software and research: IBM set up research laboratories in India in 1998 and 2001, co-located with its services business. In India it serves domestic clients as well as global delivery work, offering services spanning consulting, cloud, artificial intelligence, infrastructure and business process services to organisations across industries.

details.name: Accenture
details.description: Accenture has been operating in India since 1987, in its earlier avatar as the consulting arm of Arthur Andersen, and set up its first information technology and business process delivery centres in India in 2001, beginning in Mumbai. India is part of Accenture's global delivery network through its Advanced Technology Centers in India (ATCI), which by 2024 operated in Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Pune, Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Indore, Coimbatore, Nagpur and Bhubaneswar. The centres deliver technology services for clients across industries, with work in cloud, data and artificial intelligence, including generative AI, alongside Accenture's strategy, consulting, technology and operations services.

details.name: Samsung
details.description: Samsung India was established in 1995. It laid the foundation stone of its Noida plant in 1996, began television production there in 1997, added refrigerator production in 2003 and started making mobile phones at Noida in 2007. Samsung India also operates a second manufacturing plant at Sriperumbudur in Tamil Nadu. Its corporate headquarters are at Two Horizon Center in Gurugram, Haryana. In India, Samsung sells mobile phones and tablets, televisions and home appliances, including refrigerators and washing machines, through its Samsung India online store and retail network, supported by research and development and design facilities in India.

The three companies merged in 1956 to form Hindustan Lever Limited, which was renamed Hindustan Unilever Limited in 2007. HUL makes and sells fast-moving consumer goods in India across foods, cleaning agents, personal care and skin care, with brands including Sunlight, Lifebuoy, Surf, Lux and Sunsilk, and runs research facilities in Mumbai and Bengaluru.

details.name: Ring-necked pheasant
details.description: The ring-necked pheasant, also called the common pheasant, is the best-known game bird in the world. It began in Asia and has been introduced so widely, across Europe and North America, that many people meet it before any native species. A cock is unmistakable: glossy bottle-green head, bright red face, a crisp white collar, coppery barred body and a very long, barred tail that streams behind it in flight. Hens are quieter, mottled sandy brown all over, which hides them on the ground nest. Pheasants live along woodland edges, hedgerows, reedbeds and rough farmland, feeding on seeds, grain, berries and insects. They prefer to run from danger and only burst into the air, wings whirring, when pressed closely.

details.name: Grey partridge
details.description: The grey partridge is a plump, ground-hugging bird of open farmland across Europe and central Asia, also introduced to North America. It is mostly soft grey and brown, with an orange-brown face, finely barred flanks and, on the male, a dark chestnut horseshoe mark on the belly. Grey partridges pair up in spring, then gather into family parties called coveys for autumn and winter, feeding together on seeds, shoots and fallen grain, with insects especially important for growing chicks. Their flight is a low, fast whirr of wings broken by long glides. Once among the commonest farmland birds, they have thinned out where farming became very intensive, so a covey rising from a stubbly field margin is now a sight worth pausing for.

details.name: Chukar partridge
details.description: The chukar is a partridge of dry, rocky hillsides, ranging from the eastern Mediterranean through west and central Asia into the north-western Himalaya, including the arid slopes of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. It is a handsome bird: sandy grey above, with bold black-and-white barred flanks, a black band that runs through the eye and down to frame the white throat, and coral-red bill and legs. Chukars live in coveys on steep, stony ground dotted with scrub, feeding on seeds, leaves and insects. Their ringing, chuckling calls, which give the bird its name, carry far across a hillside at dawn. When disturbed they usually run uphill, fast and sure-footed, and only take wing to glide down across a gully.

details.name: Grey francolin
details.description: The grey francolin is one of the most familiar ground birds of the Indian subcontinent, at home in dry scrub, thorn forest edges, fallow fields and the rough ground around villages. It is finely patterned grey-brown all over, barred and speckled so closely that it seems to dissolve into dry grass, with a short chestnut tail that shows when it runs. Grey francolins go about in pairs or small family parties, scratching for seeds, shoots and insects and dust-bathing on bare patches. They are far more often heard than seen: at dawn and dusk the male throws out a loud, ringing series of notes from a stone or low bush. When flushed, they rocket away low and fast into the nearest cover.

details.name: Black francolin
details.description: The black francolin is the striking counterpart of its grey cousin, found in grasslands, reed edges and scrub near water from northern India westwards to the Middle East. A male in good light is hard to confuse with anything else: glossy black head and underparts, a bold white cheek patch, a chestnut collar, and white spotting scattered over the black back and flanks. Females are mottled brown and far harder to spot. Black francolins keep to thick cover in pairs or small groups, feeding on seeds, shoots and insects, and the male advertises himself with a loud, buzzing, ringing call delivered from a mound or bush top. It is the state bird of Haryana, and a protected species in India like all wild francolins.

details.name: Common quail
details.description: The common quail is a tiny, secretive game bird with an outsized secret: unlike most of its stay-at-home relatives, it is a true long-distance migrant, breeding across Europe and central Asia and travelling at night to winter in Africa and the Indian subcontinent. Streaked buff and brown from crown to tail, with a pale stripe over the eye and, on the male, a dark anchor mark on the throat, it is built for hiding in grass and standing crops. Almost nobody sees one well. What gives it away is the male's far-carrying three-note whistle, traditionally rendered as 'wet-my-lips', repeated from deep cover on summer evenings. If you do flush one, it rises almost from underfoot and drops back into cover within metres.

details.name: Red junglefowl
details.description: The red junglefowl is the wild ancestor of every domestic chicken on Earth, and seeing a pure wild bird in the forests of north-east and central India, or in South-East Asia, is seeing a familiar farmyard shape returned to its original life. A cock is a slim, athletic version of a gamecock: red comb and wattles, a mane of golden-orange hackle feathers, a dark body and an arched, glossy green-black tail. Hens are small and drab brown. Junglefowl feed on the forest floor, scratching through leaf litter for seeds, shoots and insects, and fly up into trees to roost at night. Forest clearance and mixing with free-ranging village chickens are the main worries for pure wild populations, so unspoilt forest birds matter.

details.name: Himalayan snowcock
details.description: The Himalayan snowcock is one of the highest-living game birds in the world, a big, heavy partridge relative of alpine slopes roughly between 3,600 and 5,000 metres, from Kashmir through Nepal to Bhutan. Its plumage is a study in camouflage: soft grey-brown above, finely streaked with chestnut and black, a pale face and a white throat patch edged with chestnut, all of which vanishes against lichen-spotted rock. Snowcocks spend the day walking steadily uphill as they feed on alpine shoots, bulbs and seeds, whistling mournfully across the slope, and when they need to change ground they launch into long, sweeping glides down into the next valley. Few watchers ever see one closely, which makes an unhurried view above the treeline a Himalayan highlight.

details.name: Red grouse
details.description: The red grouse is the moorland specialist of Britain and Ireland, a rich red-brown bird of open heather country that differs from its willow ptarmigan relatives by never turning white in winter. Males show a bright red comb above the eye, most obvious in the breeding season, and both sexes are barred and mottled to match the heather. Red grouse feed largely on young heather shoots, with berries and insects in season, and they hold small territories on the moor through the year. Their alarm call, a harsh, accelerating 'go-back, go-back', is one of the classic sounds of northern uplands. Heather moorland management is debated by conservationists, so the most rewarding views are of undisturbed birds watched quietly from paths and tracks.

details.name: Willow ptarmigan
details.description: The willow ptarmigan is the circumpolar grouse of tundra and willow scrub, found right around the northern hemisphere from Alaska and Canada to Scandinavia and Siberia. Its whole life is shaped by snow: in winter it turns pure white except for a black tail, with heavily feathered feet that work like snowshoes, while in summer it moults into a mottled chestnut-brown that matches bare tundra. Males in spring show a rich red-brown head and neck against the still-white body. Willow ptarmigan feed on willow and birch buds and shoots in winter and add leaves, berries and insects in summer. The red grouse of Britain and Ireland is its close island relative, adapted to a milder climate that rarely demands a white winter coat.

details.name: Western capercaillie
details.description: The western capercaillie is the giant of the grouse family, a bird the size of a small turkey that lives in old conifer forests from Scotland, where it was reintroduced, across northern Europe to Siberia. A cock in display is a dramatic sight: dark slate plumage with a metallic green sheen, a huge tail fanned upright, and a strange song of clicks and pops ending in a sound like a cork leaving a bottle, performed at communal display grounds called leks at dawn. Hens are barred brown and much smaller. Capercaillie feed on pine needles in winter and bilberries, shoots and insects in summer. Numbers have fallen in much of Europe, and displaying birds are easily disturbed, so leks should only ever be watched from a respectful distance, if at all.

details.name: Wild turkey
details.description: The wild turkey is North America's great game bird, far larger and more athletic than its domestic descendants. A gobbler carries iridescent bronze-green plumage, a broad tail that fans into a rust-tipped semicircle in display, a blue and red bare head whose colours shift with excitement, and a dangling 'beard' of coarse feathers on the chest. Hens are slimmer and duller. Wild turkeys live in woodland mixed with clearings and fields, feeding on acorns, seeds, grasses and insects, and despite their bulk they fly strongly to roost high in trees at night. Hunted almost to vanishing point by the early twentieth century, they were brought back by one of the great conservation restoration programmes and are now a common, if wary, sight again.

details.name: Helmeted guineafowl
details.description: The helmeted guineafowl is Africa's contribution to the classic game birds, a flocking bird of savanna and open woodland that has also been domesticated and carried around the world. Its body is pearl-grey and densely spotted with white, like a star field, and its bare head carries blue and red skin topped by the bony casque, or 'helmet', that gives the species its name. Guineafowl spend the day walking in noisy parties, scratching for seeds, bulbs and insects, and they are famous lookouts: any predator or stranger triggers an outbreak of harsh, rattling alarm calls. At dusk the flock flies, heavily but willingly, up into trees to roost. Wild birds remain common across much of sub-Saharan Africa wherever cover and water are both within reach.

details.name: Northern bobwhite
details.description: The northern bobwhite is the classic quail of eastern and central North America, a small, plump bird of grassland, hedgerows and open pine woods. The cock has a bold pattern of a white stripe through the eye and a white throat, set against mottled chestnut and grey; the hen wears the same pattern in buff. Its name comes straight from its clear, whistled call, 'bob-white', which rises from field edges on spring mornings. Bobwhites live in tight winter groups called coveys, famously roosting on the ground in a tight circle, tails together and heads facing outwards, ready to scatter in every direction. Like many grassland birds it has declined as field margins and rough ground have been tidied away, so its whistle is heard less often than it was.

summary: Compare yoga mats by practice style, grip when dry or sweaty, thickness, density, size, material, odour, cleaning, and carrying weight.

details.name: Natural rubber mat
details.description: Natural rubber mats are made from tapped tree rubber, usually with a PU or microfibre top layer bonded over a solid rubber base. The material is dense, so these mats lie completely flat, grip the floor hard and give strong hand and foot traction that holds up in dynamic and sweaty practice, with firm, grounded cushioning rather than a soft, spongy feel. They suit regular practitioners and hot-yoga users who prioritise grip and stability. They are heavier to carry, can smell of rubber at first, need airing before use, and should be kept out of strong sunlight.

details.name: TPE mat
details.description: TPE mats are made from thermoplastic elastomer, a soft, rubber-like material usually built as a dual-layer, dual-colour sheet with textured surfaces on both sides. They are noticeably lighter than rubber or PVC mats of the same thickness, give comfortable, springy cushioning for knees and joints, and provide reliable dry grip for everyday practice, which is why they are a popular first mat for home use. TPE suits beginners, home practitioners and anyone carrying a mat to a class. Avoid leaving one in heat or strong sun, wipe it clean after use, and check the textured surface has not worn smooth.

details.description: PVC mats are the long-established workhorse of yoga mats, made from polyvinyl chloride in a wide range of thicknesses, colours and price bands. The material is tough, resists tearing and abrasion, wipes clean easily and keeps its slightly sticky surface feel for years, which is why studios and schools often buy PVC in bulk. Grip is good for general practice, though very sweaty hands can still slip. PVC suits beginners, studios and budget buyers who want durability above all. A new mat can smell at first, so air it before use, and note that PVC is not biodegradable.

details.name: Site search
details.description: Site search is the fastest way into everything already published on VisitBest. Start with the words you would naturally use for the product, company, place or person you have in mind, then open the most relevant results and check their titles and summaries before reading in full. If a first search returns too much, add a category word, a brand or a place name to narrow it. If it returns too little, try a shorter phrase or a common synonym instead. Search results are a starting point, not a verdict: open the guide itself, check when it was updated, and follow any links it gives to the original source before you act on it.

details.name: Product comparison checklist
details.description: A comparison only helps if every option is judged on the same points, so record the same fields for each product before deciding. Note what it must fit or work with, the specifications that matter for your actual use, what warranty or support is offered, who the seller is, and the full cost once every necessary charge is counted. Leave out features you will never use, however impressive they look in a listing. When two options are close, revisit your original requirements rather than chasing a small specification difference. Keep the written comparison with the shortlist, so a later price or stock change can be checked against the same evidence.

details.name: Company research checklist
details.description: Before asking any company for a proposal, establish who you would actually be dealing with. Confirm the trading name and the legal entity behind it, where the company is based and which areas it serves, and whether it genuinely works in the service category you need. Ask what comparable work it has done and whether references or examples can be checked independently, rather than taken from its own marketing alone. Read any proposed contract for scope, payment stages, timelines and what happens if the work changes or is cancelled. Record each check with its source and date, so the shortlist can be revisited if a detail changes before you commit.

details.name: Source-quality checklist
details.description: Good decisions rest on sources that can be checked, so test every important claim before reusing it. Confirm when the source was published or last updated, who wrote it, and what evidence it actually shows rather than merely asserts. Wherever possible, follow a claim back to its primary source: an official document, an original announcement or first-hand reporting. Check whether other reliable sources agree, and note any conflict instead of smoothing it over. Be especially careful with figures, dates and quotations, which are easily distorted as they are copied from page to page. If a claim cannot be traced or confirmed, label it as unverified or leave it out.

Links break in ordinary ways: a page is moved or renamed, a guide is retired or combined with another, or an address is typed incorrectly when the link is added. title: Miniature Horses: Size, Temperament, Care and Ownership
summary: A beginner's guide to miniature horses, including what ‘miniature’ means, daily care, fencing, diet, hoof care, companionship, and realistic costs.
editorial: Miniature horses are equines, not house pets or scaled-down dogs. They need suitable outdoor space, another compatible equine companion, professional hoof and dental care, and careful weight management.
items: Safe boundaries without gaps designed only for full-size horses
Obesity and metabolic risk require professional guidance
Regular social contact with a compatible equine
Human attention alone is usually not enough
Routine trimming by an experienced farrier
Small hooves still need scheduled care

details.name: What counts as a miniature horse
details.description: “Miniature” is about height, not about being a pony. A miniature horse is a horse in proportion — refined head, long legs and a light body — bred down in size, and measured at the last hairs of the mane on top of the withers. Registry limits are commonly around 34 to 38 inches (roughly 86–97 cm) depending on the registry and division. The photograph shows two miniatures beside an ordinary horse, which gives the true scale better than any number. Most adults weigh roughly 70–160 kg (150–350 lb). Despite their size they are horses, not pets, with a horse’s needs and a typical lifespan of 25 years or more.
details.imageAlt: An ordinary horse standing behind a fence beside two miniature horses, showing the size difference

details.name: Temperament and handling
details.description: Well-bred miniatures are typically people-oriented, curious and quick to learn, which is why they are popular for therapy visits and simply as companion animals. The photograph, taken at a Franciscan monastery in Texas that raises miniature horses, shows the quiet, trusting behaviour that patient handling produces. But temperament varies between individuals, and a miniature is still a horse: it can startle, nip or kick if it is frightened or roughly handled, and stallions need experienced management. Handle youngsters gently and regularly, set clear boundaries from the start, supervise children closely, and never lift, carry or dress up a miniature as if it were a toy.
details.imageAlt: A Franciscan sister hand-feeding a chestnut miniature horse in a field in Brenham, Texas

details.name: Secure fencing
details.description: A miniature needs fencing designed at its own height, not a full-size horse’s. Gaps beneath rails and gates that a big horse would ignore can let a miniature slip out, or trap a leg or head, so walk the boundary at miniature eye level and close every gap. Sturdy post-and-rail, equine mesh, or well-maintained electric fencing all work; avoid barbed wire, which can tear skin and manes at exactly the height a miniature moves. Gates must latch firmly, because many miniatures learn to test and worry at loose fittings. Check regularly for protruding bolts, sharp edges and rotten posts, and provide simple shelter from wind and driving rain.
details.imageAlt: A pinto miniature horse galloping across a pasture with an electric fence behind it

details.name: Forage-led diet
details.description: A miniature’s diet should be built on forage: grass and hay, and little else for most healthy adults. Miniatures are famously easy keepers, shaped by sparse grazing, so rich pasture and generous hard feed quickly lead to obesity, laminitis (founder) and metabolic disease. Many owners restrict grazing with a muzzle, strip grazing or a bare “dry lot”, and weigh hay rather than guessing by eye; a common starting point is around 1.5–2% of bodyweight in forage per day, adjusted with veterinary advice. Keep concentrates minimal unless a vet advises otherwise, provide constant clean water and a salt or mineral lick, introduce feed changes gradually, and condition-score regularly so weight creep is caught early.
details.imageAlt: A miniature horse grazing in a paddock near Cottingham, England

details.name: Companionship
details.description: Horses are herd animals, and miniature horses are no exception. A single miniature kept alone often becomes stressed, vocal or withdrawn, however much human attention it receives. The best companion is another miniature or a small, gentle pony of similar size, so that neither animal is bullied away from hay or shelter; pairs and small groups graze, rest and groom together, as the horses in the photograph are doing. Introduce new companions gradually, at first over a fence, and watch feeding times, where differences in size and confidence show most. A miniature can live with full-size horses, but gates, fencing heights and feed buckets must suit the smallest animal.
details.imageAlt: A mare and three miniature horses greeting each other beside a fence under a tree

details.name: Hoof care
details.description: Miniature hooves are ordinary horse hooves in miniature: they grow continuously and need routine trimming by a farrier, typically every six to eight weeks. Before you buy, find a farrier who is happy to work at miniature height, because not every professional will. Between visits, pick out the feet regularly and check for packed stones, cracks, heat or the sour smell of thrush, which thrives in wet bedding and mud. Overgrown feet quickly distort leg angles in such small animals, and horses bred extremely small can have limb and joint problems that need veterinary input. Keep a simple record of trim dates and any lameness, however mild it seems.
details.imageAlt: A farrier trimming a horse’s hind hoof with a hoof knife

details.name: Dental and veterinary care
details.description: A miniature carries a full set of horse teeth in a small jaw, so crowding, retained baby teeth and uneven wear are common. Arrange dental checks at least once a year with a veterinarian or a qualified equine dental technician, who can rasp (“float”) the sharp points that cut the cheeks and tongue, as in the photograph. Register with an equine vet before an emergency, and keep up the usual preventive care: vaccinations, and worming guided by faecal egg counts rather than by habit. Colic, choke and laminitis present just as they do in full-size horses, and older miniatures can develop hormonal conditions such as Cushing’s disease, another reason for regular checks.
details.imageAlt: An equine dental technician examining a horse’s teeth with a headlamp and mouth speculum

details.name: Training and enrichment
details.description: Miniatures learn exactly like horses, and training is both enrichment and exercise. Start with the essentials: catching, haltering, leading politely, standing still for the farrier and vet, and loading into transport. Beyond the basics, many miniatures are trained to drive — pulling a light cart is their classic job, as shown in the photograph — and to work obstacle courses, liberty routines and groundwork games that keep minds and bodies busy. A few are even trained for therapy visits or as guide animals. Keep sessions short, calm and consistent. Miniatures are not riding horses for adults, and regular activity is one of the best defences against weight gain.
details.imageAlt: A miniature horse in harness pulling a two-seat driving cart in an arena

details.name: Falabella
details.description: The Falabella is one of the smallest horse breeds in the world, developed in Argentina by the Falabella family from the nineteenth century onwards, using small Thoroughbred, Criollo and Shetland-type stock. Most stand only about 28–34 inches (71–86 cm) at the withers, yet they are built like small horses rather than ponies, often with notably thick manes and tails, like the zoo-kept horse in the photograph. Falabellas are long-lived, hardy and intelligent, and are kept as companion animals, show horses and therapy animals. Because they have been bred so small, responsible breeders watch carefully for soundness, and their care — feeding, fencing, hoof and dental work — is the same as any miniature’s.
details.imageAlt: A palomino Falabella miniature horse with a long flaxen mane standing in a paddock at Shoushan Zoo

details.name: American Miniature Horse
details.description: The American Miniature Horse was developed in the United States during the twentieth century from Shetland pony, Falabella, and small Thoroughbred and Appaloosa bloodlines. The goal was a true horse in miniature — balanced, refined and athletic, like the registered grey stallion in the photograph. The American Miniature Horse Association, founded in 1978, registers horses up to 34 inches at the withers, while the American Miniature Horse Registry also recognises a taller division up to 38 inches. American Miniatures are shown in halter, driving, jumping and obstacle classes, work as therapy animals, and are now bred in many countries well beyond the United States.
details.imageAlt: A grey American Miniature Horse stallion standing in tall grass

details.name: Miniature Shetland Pony
details.description: The Miniature Shetland is a scaled-down Shetland pony, the hardy breed from Scotland’s Shetland Islands. Where a standard Shetland stands up to about 42 inches, miniatures are generally bred under roughly 34–35 inches, keeping the breed’s sturdy pony proportions: a compact body, short strong legs, and a thick double coat with an abundant mane and tail that shrugs off harsh island weather. The young horse in the photograph lives at a German wildlife park. Miniature Shetlands are strong for their size, famously independent-minded, and popular in Britain and Europe as children’s ponies, driving ponies and companions. Like all miniatures, they gain weight easily and need careful grazing management.
details.imageAlt: A young chestnut Miniature Shetland Pony standing on grass at Wildpark Schwentinental

title: Best Bike Racks for Cars: Roof, Hitch and Trunk Options Compared
summary: Choose a cycle carrier by car compatibility, number and weight of bikes, loading height, frame contact, security, visibility, and local regulations.
editorial: A rack must be approved for both the vehicle and the bicycle load. Confirm roof limits, hitch ratings, hatch clearance, lights, and number-plate visibility before driving.

details.name: Roof-mounted rack
details.description: A roof-mounted rack carries bikes upright on crossbars fitted to the car's roof rails or to approved roof-rack feet. Each bike is held by its frame, fork or front wheel, so the boot, rear doors, lights and number plate stay completely clear. The costs are lifting every bike to roof height, checking the car's roof load rating against rack plus bikes, more wind noise, and remembering the extra height at garages, height barriers and low branches. It suits regular riders with a suitable roof system who value clear rear access.

details.name: Hitch platform rack
details.description: A hitch platform rack slots into a rated tow hitch receiver and carries bikes on wheel trays, with each bike supported under its tyres and held by a wheel hook or frame arm. Loading is low and easy, bikes sit apart without touching, and many models tilt for boot access or fold up when empty. It only works on a vehicle fitted with a correctly rated hitch, which is uncommon on Indian cars, and buyers must check combined bike weight, hitch limits, and whether lights and plate remain visible.

details.name: Hitch hanging rack
details.description: A hitch hanging rack slots into a tow hitch receiver and carries bikes hanging from two support arms, with frames resting in cradles and strapped in place. It can carry several conventional-frame bikes in a compact, relatively light package and often tilts or folds for storage and boot access. Frames touch the cradles, so padding matters, bikes can sway or contact each other, and step-through, small or unusual frames may need an adapter bar. It needs a correctly rated hitch, and total bike weight, lights and plate visibility must be checked.
details.modelTitle: Allen Sports 3-Bike Hitch Racks for 1 1/4 in. and 2 in. Hitch

details.name: Trunk-mounted rack
details.description: A trunk-mounted rack straps and hooks onto the boot lid, hatch or rear door, with padded feet resting against the car and bikes held on support arms. It needs no hitch or roof bars, folds flat for storage, and is the easiest type to buy and fit in India for occasional trips. Fit is vehicle-specific, so maker approval matters, straps must be rechecked, and padding is essential to protect paint. Boot access is usually blocked, rear wiper and spoiler fit can rule cars out, and lights and plate must stay visible.
details.modelTitle: Universal Rear Mounted Car Bike Rack for SUVs, Sedans and Hatchbacks - Safely Carries 3 Bikes
details.imageAlt: Universal Rear Mounted Car Bike Rack for SUVs, Sedans and Hatchbacks - Safely Carries 3 Bikes — Trunk-mounted rack bike rack

details.name: Spare-wheel rack
details.description: A spare-wheel rack mounts over or through the rear spare wheel fitted to SUVs such as those with a tailgate-mounted spare, using the wheel as its support instead of a hitch or straps on body panels. Bikes sit on carry arms behind the spare, keeping the roof and tow point free. The spare, its carrier and the rear door hinges then carry the extra load, so wheel condition, total weight and door operation must be checked carefully, the door may not open normally with bikes loaded, and lights and plate must remain visible.
details.modelTitle: Allen Sports Deluxe 2-Bike Spare Tire Rack, Black

Bikes stay out of the airflow, no hitch or roof system is needed, and loading is at waist height. Bed space is used up, forks, frames and the tailgate need padding and protection against rubbing, bikes should be strapped and locked in the open bed, and any load overhanging the rear must keep lights and plate visible.

details.name: Arabian
details.description: The Arabian is one of the oldest and most influential breeds, developed on the Arabian Peninsula by Bedouin tribes who prized stamina, hardiness and courage in desert conditions. It is a small, refined horse, typically standing 14.1 to 15.1 hands (about 145–155 cm), with a distinctive dished face, wide forehead, arched neck and high tail carriage. Despite its size it is famously tough, with dense bone and excellent endurance, and it passes its qualities strongly to its offspring — most modern light breeds carry Arabian blood. Arabians are intelligent and spirited, and they excel at endurance racing, where they dominate at the top level, as well as showing, pleasure riding and breeding programmes worldwide.
details.imageAlt: A black Arabian stallion standing in profile on grass

details.name: Thoroughbred
details.description: The Thoroughbred was developed in England in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, when Arabian, Barb and Turkoman stallions were crossed with native mares; every modern Thoroughbred traces to foundation sires of that era. It typically stands 15.2 to 17 hands (about 157–173 cm) and is a lean, athletic, long-legged horse built for speed over distance. Thoroughbreds are the world's racehorses, contesting flat and jump racing on every continent, and their athleticism also makes them prized for eventing, show jumping and polo. They are sensitive, energetic horses — often described as "hot" — so they usually suit experienced riders, though retrained ex-racehorses also become popular riding horses.
details.imageAlt: A bay Thoroughbred horse standing in a stable yard

details.name: American Quarter Horse
details.description: The American Quarter Horse is the most numerous breed in the United States, named for its explosive speed over a quarter of a mile, a distance at which colonial sprint horses excelled. It typically stands 14.3 to 16 hands (about 150–163 cm) and is heavily muscled, with a compact body, strong hindquarters and a calm, sensible temperament. Developed into the classic horse of the western ranch, it remains the benchmark for cattle work, reining, barrel racing, rodeo events and trail riding. The breed's steady mind and versatility also make it one of the most popular family and pleasure horses in North America, and registered numbers worldwide run into the millions.
details.imageAlt: A chestnut American Quarter Horse being ridden in an outdoor arena

details.name: Andalusian
details.description: The Andalusian, officially the Pura Raza Española (Pure Spanish Horse), comes from the Iberian Peninsula, where horses of this type have been bred in Spain for centuries and were once the riding horse of Europe's courts. It typically stands 15 to 16.1 hands (about 152–165 cm), with a strong, compact build, a thick mane and tail, and grey as the most common colour. Andalusians are known for proud, elevated movement, a docile yet spirited temperament and great agility, qualities that suit them to classical dressage, high-school riding, driving and parade work. Carefully controlled by a state-run stud book, the breed is also the foundation of many other Iberian and American breeds.
details.imageAlt: A grey Andalusian horse grazing in a green field

details.name: Friesian
details.description: The Friesian comes from Friesland in the Netherlands and is one of Europe's oldest breeds, nearly lost in the early 20th century before dedicated breeders revived it. It stands 15 to 17 hands (about 152–173 cm) and is always black, with a long, wavy mane and tail and characteristic feathering on the lower legs. Friesians were once war and carriage horses; today their striking appearance and high-stepping trot make them favourites for driving, dressage, showing and film work. They are generally gentle, willing and people-oriented. Because the modern breed descends from a small number of survivors, breeders watch inbreeding carefully, and buyers should check a horse's papers and health records.
details.imageAlt: A black Friesian horse under saddle in an arena

details.name: Clydesdale
details.description: The Clydesdale is Scotland's heavy draught breed, developed in the Clyde valley in the 18th century from Flemish stallions crossed with local mares. It is a big, powerful horse, typically 16 to 18 hands (about 163–183 cm), usually bay or brown with extensive white markings and abundant silky feathering around its large feet. Bred to haul coal, farm wagons and brewery drays, Clydesdales became famous worldwide as parade and show draught horses, and exported breeding stock helped shape draught horses in North America and Australia. Despite their size they are known for a kind, steady temperament and an active, showy walk. Numbers are much reduced since the mechanisation of farming, and the breed is watched by rare-breeds organisations.
details.imageAlt: A bay Clydesdale horse with white leg feathering walking in a paddock

details.name: Appaloosa
details.description: The Appaloosa is an American breed famous for its spotted coat, which appears in patterns such as leopard (spots over the whole body) and blanket (a white area over the hips, often with spots). Horses with these colours were developed by the Nez Perce people of the Palouse region in the Pacific Northwest — the source of the breed's name. It typically stands 14.2 to 16 hands (about 147–163 cm) and is a sturdy, versatile stock horse; other breed traits include mottled skin, striped hooves and a visible white sclera around the eye. Appaloosas are used for western riding, trail riding, ranch work and showing, and are valued for hardiness and a willing temperament.
details.imageAlt: A leopard-spotted Appaloosa horse wearing a western saddle

details.name: Morgan
details.description: The Morgan is one of the oldest American breeds, descended from a single foundation stallion — a bay colt foaled in 1789, later known as Justin Morgan after his owner — whose offspring inherited his compact strength and versatility. Morgans typically stand 14.1 to 15.2 hands (about 145–157 cm) and are strongly built, with an expressive head, crested neck and kind, tractable temperament. In the 19th century Morgans did everything: ploughing, stagecoach work, cavalry service and road racing. Today the breed is a true all-rounder, used for driving, dressage, western and pleasure riding, and Morgan blood contributed to several later American breeds, including the Standardbred and the American Saddlebred.
details.imageAlt: A Morgan horse in harness pulling a show carriage

details.name: Hanoverian
details.description: The Hanoverian is Germany's best-known warmblood, developed in the Hanover region, where a state stud at Celle was founded in 1735 to improve horses for farming and cavalry. Modern breeding has refocused it entirely on sport. Hanoverians typically stand 15.3 to 17.2 hands (about 160–178 cm) and are tall, elegant, athletic horses with powerful movement and a trainable temperament. They are among the most successful breeds in international dressage and show jumping, appearing regularly on Olympic and championship teams, and are also used for eventing and driving. Selection is strict: stallions and mares must pass performance tests and inspections before entering the stud book, which keeps quality and soundness under constant review.
details.imageAlt: A bay Hanoverian horse performing dressage with its rider

details.name: Mustang
details.description: The mustang is the free-roaming horse of the western United States, descended from horses brought by Spanish colonists in the 16th century and shaped by centuries of survival in the wild. Mustangs are not a man-made breed but a feral population, and they vary in type; most are small and hardy, typically 14 to 15 hands (about 142–152 cm), with strong feet, good bone and notable sure-footedness. Wild herds on public land are managed by the US Bureau of Land Management, and surplus animals are offered for adoption. Adopted mustangs, once gentled and trained, are used for trail riding, endurance and ranch work, and are valued for toughness and intelligence.
details.imageAlt: A group of Kiger Mustangs running together in a field

details.name: Percheron
details.description: The Percheron is a French draught breed from the Perche region, west of Paris, where its ancestors hauled stagecoaches and worked farms for centuries; Arabian influence is often credited for its relatively elegant head. It typically stands 15.2 to 17.2 hands (about 157–178 cm), is heavily muscled yet active for its size, and is usually grey or black. Percherons pulled artillery and omnibuses in the 19th century and became one of the most popular draught breeds in North America. Today they are used for farm work, logging, carriage driving, parades and showing, and are crossed with lighter breeds to produce strong riding and sport horses. They are known for a willing, alert temperament.
details.imageAlt: Two grey Percheron draught horses standing at a stable

details.name: Shire
details.description: The Shire is England's great draught breed and one of the tallest and heaviest horses in the world: geldings typically stand 16 to 18 hands (about 163–183 cm) and can weigh around a tonne, with feathered legs and large, kind eyes. Developed from the medieval "great horse" that carried armoured knights and later refined for farm and brewery haulage, Shires pulled the heavy loads of industrial Britain before engines replaced them. The breed came close to disappearing in the mid-20th century and is still classed as at risk by rare-breeds bodies. Surviving Shires are used for showing, promotional brewery work, carriage driving, logging and leisure riding, and are prized for their gentle, docile nature.
details.imageAlt: A grey Shire horse in harness working in woodland

details.name: Akhal-Teke
details.description: The Akhal-Teke comes from Turkmenistan, where it was bred by nomadic tribes in the Karakum desert and is now the country's national treasure. It is a slim, elegant riding horse, typically 14.2 to 16 hands (about 147–163 cm), famous for the metallic, golden sheen of its coat, a result of the structure of its hair. Bred for speed and endurance over harsh ground, Akhal-Tekes are hardy, sensitive and famously loyal to a single rider. They compete in endurance, racing, dressage and show jumping, and performed at the highest level in Olympic dressage in the Soviet era. The breed remains rare, with carefully guarded pedigrees and only a few thousand horses worldwide.
details.imageAlt: A chestnut Akhal-Teke stallion standing with its handler

details.name: Marwari
details.description: The Marwari is India's best-known indigenous breed, from the Marwar region of Rajasthan, where it was the war horse of Rajput cavalry. Its most recognisable feature is its ears, which curve inwards until the tips may touch — a trait shared by few breeds in the world. Marwaris typically stand 14.2 to 16 hands (about 147–163 cm) and are lean, hardy horses adapted to desert heat, with a naturally proud carriage and a comfortable, ground-covering gait. Hardy and spirited, the breed declined during the 20th century but has been revived by Indian breeders and the state; Marwaris are now used for riding, endurance, polo, ceremonial duties and religious processions.
details.imageAlt: A dark Marwari stallion standing in profile outdoors

details.name: Kathiawari
details.description: The Kathiawari comes from the Kathiawar peninsula of Gujarat, on India's western coast, where it was bred as a tough cavalry and riding horse able to thrive on sparse desert forage. Like the Marwari, it has distinctive curved ears, though the breed is usually slightly smaller, typically 14.2 to 15 hands (about 147–152 cm). Kathiawaris are lean, deep-chested and remarkably hardy, known for endurance, sure-footedness on rough ground and a loyal but spirited temperament. They often show a natural pacing (amble) gait that makes long rides comfortable. In India the breed is used for riding, endurance events, mounted police work and traditional games such as tent pegging.
details.imageAlt: Two chestnut Kathiawari horses standing with their handler

details.name: Lusitano
details.description: The Lusitano is Portugal's counterpart to Spain's Andalusian: an Iberian breed, named for Lusitania, the Roman province that covered much of modern Portugal. It typically stands 15 to 16.1 hands (about 152–165 cm), with a slightly convex profile, a powerful hindquarter and a calm, brave temperament. For centuries it was bred for mounted bullfighting and classical riding, work that demands agility, balance and courage; today Lusitanos excel in dressage, working equitation — a discipline Portugal leads — driving and leisure riding. The breed is known for comfortable, collected gaits and a strong ability to gather weight onto its hindquarters, which makes advanced movements such as piaffe come naturally to it.
details.imageAlt: Head and neck portrait of a grey Lusitano horse with a long mane

details.name: American Paint Horse
details.description: The American Paint Horse combines the build of a western stock horse with pinto colouring — large white markings mixed with another colour, in patterns called tobiano (smooth-edged patches, white crossing the back) and overo (jagged patches that usually do not cross the back). It typically stands 14.2 to 16.2 hands (about 147–168 cm) and is muscular and athletic, closely related to the Quarter Horse and Thoroughbred, from which registered Paints must descend. A spotted horse that meets the pedigree rules is a Paint; a similar-looking horse without them is a pinto, which is a colour type, not a breed. Paints are popular for western showing, ranch work, trail riding and pleasure riding.
details.imageAlt: A tobiano American Paint Horse being led in an arena

details.name: Shetland Pony
details.description: The Shetland Pony comes from the Shetland Islands off northern Scotland, where ponies adapted to harsh weather and sparse grazing over many centuries. It is one of the smallest equines, typically 9 to 10.2 hands (about 92–107 cm) in the British standard, yet pound for pound it is among the strongest, able to pull far more than its size suggests. Shetlands worked in crofts and, in the 19th century, in coal mines as pit ponies. They have a thick double coat, a full mane and tail and a reputation for intelligence and independence — sometimes described as stubborn. Today they are classic children's ponies and driving ponies, but they need firm handling and careful weight management.
details.imageAlt: A black Shetland pony with a pale mane standing in a field

title: Water Birds: Herons, Ducks, Waders and Divers of Lakes, Rivers and Coasts
summary: A guide to 18 recognisable water birds — herons, egrets, ducks, geese, swans, kingfishers, flamingos, pelicans, cormorants, grebes, ibises, storks, cranes, gulls, terns, coots, moorhens and the osprey — with identification, habitat and behaviour for each.
editorial: Water birds are not one scientific family: the name covers unrelated birds that feed, swim or wade in wetlands, from metre-tall herons to the palm-sized kingfisher. This guide focuses on identification and responsible observation — what each bird looks like, where it lives and how it feeds — using well-established natural-history references.

details.name: Grey heron
details.description: The grey heron is one of the most familiar large wading birds of the Old World, standing about a metre tall with grey upperparts, a white head and neck, a black eyebrow stripe that extends into wispy plumes, and a dagger-like yellow bill. It waits motionless at the edge of lakes, rivers, marshes and even garden ponds, then strikes with a sudden jab of the neck to catch fish, frogs and other small animals. In flight the neck folds back into an S-shape and the broad wings beat slowly, which separates herons from storks and cranes. Grey herons usually nest colonially in tall trees in heronries, building large stick nests, and they are widespread across Europe, Asia and parts of Africa, with northern birds moving south in hard winters.

details.name: Great egret
details.description: The great egret is a tall, all-white heron found on every continent except Antarctica, easily recognised by its size, long black legs, and yellow bill that turns partly dark in the breeding season, when delicate lacy plumes trail from its back. Those plumes were once so prized for fashion that the species was hunted close to collapse in some regions, and protecting it helped inspire early bird-protection societies. It stalks slowly through shallow wetlands, flooded fields and mangroves, spearing fish, frogs, crustaceans and insects with quick thrusts of the bill. Great egrets often nest in colonies alongside other herons and egrets, building stick platforms in trees or reedbeds over water, and they have expanded their range noticeably during the last century.

details.name: Mallard
details.description: The mallard is the world's most familiar duck and the ancestor of nearly all domestic ducks. The drake is unmistakable in breeding plumage, with a glossy green head, white collar, chestnut breast and a grey body ending in curled black tail feathers, while the female is mottled brown with an orange-and-brown bill; both sexes show a blue-purple speculum edged with white on the wing. Mallards are dabbling ducks: they feed at the surface or tip tail-up to reach aquatic plants, seeds, snails and insects in ponds, marshes, rivers and city parks, and they rarely dive. Highly adaptable and largely resident where water stays unfrozen, they breed across the Northern Hemisphere, nesting on the ground near water, and females raise the striped ducklings alone.

details.name: Greylag goose
details.description: The greylag goose is the bulky ancestor of most domestic farmyard geese and the largest of the grey geese native to Europe and Asia. It is brownish-grey overall with a heavy orange-pink bill, pink legs, lighter fringes to the back feathers and a pale belly often marked with dark flecks. Greylags graze on grass, roots and cereal stubble, usually in family parties that stay together through the winter, and they are strong, vocal fliers that travel in noisy skeins between wetlands and feeding fields. Northern populations breed beside lakes and marshes in Iceland, Scandinavia and across northern Asia and migrate south for winter, while many southern birds are resident; reintroduced and feral flocks now breed widely in parks and gravel pits.

details.name: Mute swan
details.description: The mute swan is a huge, graceful white waterbird of lakes, slow rivers and coastal lagoons across Europe and Asia, widely introduced elsewhere including North America. Adults are identified by the orange bill with a prominent black knob at its base, and they often swim with the neck curved into a gentle S and wings slightly raised. Despite the name they are not silent: they hiss, snort and grunt, and their wings make a throbbing hum in flight. Mute swans feed mainly on underwater plants reached with the long neck, and pairs defend a territory fiercely while raising grey-brown cygnets on a large mound nest at the water's edge; long-term pair bonds are typical.

details.name: Common kingfisher
details.description: The common kingfisher is a small, jewel-bright bird of rivers, streams, canals and lakeshores across Europe, Asia and North Africa: electric blue-green above, rich orange below, with a long black dagger bill — females show an orange-red tint on the lower bill. It hunts from a low perch over clear, slow water, watching for small fish, then plunges headfirst and returns to beat its catch on the branch before swallowing it head-first. Kingfishers fly fast and low over the water with whirring wings and a piercing whistle. They nest in a tunnel dug into a steep earth bank, and because they need clear water and plentiful small fish, their presence is often taken as a sign of a healthy waterway.

details.name: Greater flamingo
details.description: The greater flamingo is the largest and palest of the flamingos, a tall pink wader of shallow lagoons, salt pans, estuaries and alkaline lakes around the Mediterranean, Africa and southern Asia. Its oddly bent bill — pink with a black tip — is held upside down in the water while the bird shuffles forward, filtering out algae, diatoms, tiny crustaceans and insect larvae with comb-like plates; the pink colour itself comes from carotenoid pigments in that food. Greater flamingos are intensely social, feeding and displaying in groups that can number thousands, and they breed colonially on mud mounds in the shallows, where both parents feed the chick on a milk-like secretion. In flight, neck and legs stretch out in a line and the black flight feathers flash against the pink wings.

details.name: Great white pelican
details.description: The great white pelican is one of the largest flying birds in the world, with a wingspan that can exceed three metres, brilliant white plumage, black flight feathers and an enormous orange-yellow bill with a stretchy throat pouch. It breeds in colonies around shallow lakes, deltas and marshes in south-eastern Europe, Asia and Africa, laying its eggs in a scrape on the ground. Unlike the brown pelican, it never plunge-dives: groups fish cooperatively at the surface, herding fish into the shallows and scooping them up in their pouches. Great white pelicans are superb soaring birds that ride thermals in long lines between feeding and breeding waters, and northern populations migrate long distances to warmer wintering grounds.

details.name: Great cormorant
details.description: The great cormorant is a large, dark fishing bird found on coasts and inland waters almost worldwide. Adults are blackish with a green-bronze sheen, a white throat patch and, in breeding dress, white patches on the head and thigh; the hooked bill and fully webbed feet mark it as a pursuit diver. Cormorants swim low in the water, dive from the surface and chase fish underwater, sometimes working in groups, then return to a post, rock or dead tree and stand with wings held half-open — a posture thought to help dry feathers that are less waterproof than those of most waterbirds. They nest colonially in trees, cliffs or on the ground, and inland populations have increased greatly in recent decades, which sometimes brings them into conflict with fisheries.

details.name: Great crested grebe
details.description: The great crested grebe is an elegant diving bird of lakes, reservoirs and slow rivers across Europe, Asia, Africa and Australasia, famous for its elaborate courtship: pairs face each other, shake their heads, dive and rise together, and perform a dance in which both birds rear up chest-to-chest offering beakfuls of weed. In breeding plumage it has chestnut cheek frills and black double crest tufts; in winter it is plainer grey and white. Grebes are almost entirely aquatic — their legs are set so far back that they can barely walk — and they dive to catch fish and aquatic invertebrates, building a floating nest of weed anchored to reeds. Chicks are striped and often ride on a parent's back among the feathers.

details.name: Glossy ibis
details.description: The glossy ibis is a slim, dark wading bird of marshes, rice fields, flooded meadows and estuaries, with a long, downcurved bill for probing soft mud. At a distance it looks blackish, but in good light the plumage shines chestnut, green and purple — the glossy finish that gives it its name. It feeds in small flocks, walking slowly through shallow water and feeling for insect larvae, snails, crustaceans, frogs and small fish. The glossy ibis is the most widespread ibis in the world, breeding in scattered colonies, often alongside herons and spoonbills, across southern Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia and the Americas, and its range has expanded in recent decades; northern breeders move south after the breeding season.

details.name: White stork
details.description: The white stork is a large, much-loved bird of open farmland, wet meadows and marshes across Europe, Africa and western Asia, white with black flight feathers, a long red bill and long red legs. It is famous for nesting on rooftops, chimneys, pylons and specially built platforms in villages and towns, building huge stick nests that pairs reuse and add to year after year, and for greeting its mate by throwing back its head and clattering its bill. White storks walk steadily through grassland and shallows hunting frogs, large insects, earthworms and small mammals. European birds migrate in vast soaring flocks, western birds crossing at Gibraltar and eastern birds via the Bosphorus to winter in Africa, avoiding long sea crossings by riding thermals over land.

details.name: Common crane
details.description: The common crane is a tall, stately grey bird of wetlands and farmland across northern Europe and Asia, with a black-and-white head pattern, a splash of red on the crown and a bustle of drooping inner wing feathers over the tail. Its far-carrying, trumpeting calls are among the classic sounds of wild wetlands. Cranes feed in flocks on plant material, grain, insects and small animals in shallow marshes, bogs and stubble fields, and pairs perform leaping, bowing dances with raised wings, most often in spring. They breed in undisturbed wetlands, building a mound of reeds in shallow water, and migrate in family groups along traditional routes to wintering grounds in southern Europe, Africa and southern Asia, with major staging sites where thousands gather.

details.name: European herring gull
details.description: The European herring gull is the archetypal large gull of northern coasts, harbours and seaside towns: pale grey above, white below, with black wingtips spotted white, pink legs and a strong yellow bill carrying a red spot on the lower mandible, which chicks peck to prompt feeding. It is an opportunistic omnivore, eating fish, crabs, shellfish — sometimes dropped onto rocks to break them open — eggs, refuse and scavenged scraps, and it is quick to exploit fishing boats and harbours. Herring gulls nest colonially on cliffs, islands, beaches and increasingly on flat rooftops, defending noisy territories while raising speckled chicks. Young birds take four years to reach adult plumage, passing through mottled brown stages that make gull identification a famous challenge.

details.name: Common tern
details.description: The common tern is a slim, graceful seabird of coasts, lakes and rivers across the Northern Hemisphere, silvery grey and white with a black cap, deeply forked tail and a red bill usually tipped with black. It hunts by hovering over the water and plunge-diving for small fish and crustaceans, often in loose, noisy flocks. Common terns breed in colonies on beaches, shingle banks, islands and even flat roofs or rafts, laying camouflaged eggs in a simple scrape and mobbing intruders boldly. They are champion migrants: birds breeding in northern Europe and North America winter off Africa and South America, and the species' close relative the Arctic tern outdoes even that. Adults take several years to breed and can live for decades.

details.name: Eurasian coot
details.description: The Eurasian coot is a stocky, soot-black waterbird of lakes, ponds, marshes and slow rivers across Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia, instantly recognised by its white bill that runs up into a white shield on the forehead — the origin of the phrase 'bald as a coot'. Its toes are lobed rather than fully webbed, an adaptation that suits both swimming and walking on floating vegetation. Coots graze on aquatic plants, algae, seeds and invertebrates, diving or upending to reach them, and they are famously quarrelsome, charging at rivals with splashing runs across the surface. Pairs build a bulky nest of reeds at the water's edge and raise black chicks with startling orange-red down on the head; adults outside breeding areas gather in large winter rafts.

details.name: Common moorhen
details.description: The common moorhen is a familiar, medium-sized waterbird of ponds, ditches, marshes and park lakes on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. Adults are dark slate-grey and brown with a white stripe along the flank, white undertail patches flashed as the bird flicks its tail, and a striking red bill with a yellow tip that extends into a red forehead shield. Moorhens swim with a jerky, nodding motion and walk delicately over lily pads and mud on long greenish legs with very long toes that spread their weight. They feed on water plants, seeds, snails, insects and other small creatures, and build a nest of reeds hidden in waterside vegetation; earlier broods sometimes stay on to help feed later chicks.

details.name: Osprey
details.description: The osprey is a fish-eating hawk found on every continent except Antarctica, dark brown above and white below, with a white head crossed by a dark eye-stripe and long, narrow wings that show a distinctive crook at the wrist when soaring. It hunts over lakes, rivers, reservoirs and coasts, hovering or circling before folding its wings and plunging feet-first into the water — its reversible outer toe and spiny foot pads help it grip slippery fish, which it turns head-first into the wind as it flies to a perch or nest. Ospreys build large stick nests on dead trees, cliffs, channel markers and purpose-built platforms, often reusing them for years. Northern populations migrate thousands of kilometres to winter in Africa, South America and southern Asia.
