details.name: Sulphur-crested cockatoo
details.description: The sulphur-crested cockatoo (Cacatua galerita) is the big white cockatoo most people picture first: snow-white plumage, a forward-curving crest of bright yellow that it raises when excited or alarmed, yellow washes under the wings and tail, and a ring of pale blue skin around the eye. It is native to northern and eastern Australia and southern New Guinea, and lives in woodland, rainforest edges, farmland and city parks. Bold, intelligent and very long-lived, it feeds on seeds, berries, nuts, roots and insect larvae, often in noisy flocks that drop to the ground to graze and post lookouts in the trees. Its screech carries for kilometres, and its powerful bill can strip bark and splinter timber. The IUCN Red List classifies the species as Least Concern, and it remains common across much of its range.

details.name: White cockatoo
details.description: The white cockatoo (Cacatua alba), also called the umbrella cockatoo, is pure white from crest to tail, with yellow only on the underside of the wings. Its party trick is the crest: a broad, semicircular fan that springs upright around the head when the bird is excited, curious or alarmed, giving the species its umbrella name. Males have dark brown or black eyes, females warmer reddish-brown ones. It is found only on the North Maluku islands of Indonesia — Halmahera, Bacan, Ternate, Tidore, Kasiruta and Mandioli — in lowland forest and mangrove edges. It feeds on fruit, seeds, nuts, berries and insects, and is gentle and quiet by cockatoo standards in the wild. Heavy trapping for the cage-bird trade and logging have hit it hard, and the IUCN Red List classifies the white cockatoo as Endangered.

details.name: Salmon-crested cockatoo
details.description: The salmon-crested cockatoo (Cacatua moluccensis), or Moluccan cockatoo, is the largest of the white cockatoos, and one of the most beautiful: white plumage washed with pink, and long crest feathers of deep salmon-pink that show fully when the crest is raised. It comes from a single island group — Seram and its neighbours in the South Maluku islands of Indonesia — where it lives in lowland rainforest, usually below 1,000 metres. It eats seeds, nuts, fruit, berries and insects, cracking hard shells in its massive bill, and travels in pairs or small, very noisy groups; its voice is among the loudest of any parrot. Decades of trapping for the pet trade, plus logging of its forest, have reduced numbers sharply. The IUCN Red List classifies the salmon-crested cockatoo as Endangered, and international trade in wild birds is banned.

details.name: Citron-crested cockatoo
details.description: The citron-crested cockatoo (Cacatua citrinocristata) is the rarest bird in this guide. It looks like a smaller sulphur-crested cockatoo, but the crest is a rich orange rather than lemon-yellow, and the ear patch is washed yellow-orange. Long treated as a subspecies of the yellow-crested cockatoo, it is now recognised as a species in its own right. It lives only on Sumba, an Indonesian island east of Bali, in dry deciduous forest, woodland and scattered trees around farmland. It feeds on seeds, fruit, berries and flowers, moving in pairs or small parties and roosting communally. Relentless trapping for the cage-bird trade has emptied much of the island, and remaining birds are confined to fragments of forest. The IUCN Red List classifies the citron-crested cockatoo as Critically Endangered — the most threatened cockatoo in this guide.

details.name: Blue-eyed cockatoo
details.description: The blue-eyed cockatoo (Cacatua ophthalmica) is named for the vivid turquoise-blue ring of bare skin around its eye, the brightest of any cockatoo. Otherwise it is a typical Cacatua: white plumage with a lemon wash under the wings and tail, a rounded, recurved white crest and a big black bill. It is found only on New Britain and New Ireland in Papua New Guinea's Bismarck Archipelago, in lowland rainforest up into the hills. It feeds on seeds, nuts, fruit, berries and insects, and is reported to be shyer and quieter than its Australian cousins, travelling in pairs or small groups through the canopy. Logging of lowland forest for timber and oil-palm planting is its main threat, along with some trapping. The IUCN Red List classifies the blue-eyed cockatoo as Vulnerable.

details.name: Ducorps's cockatoo
details.description: Ducorps's cockatoo (Cacatua ducorpsii), also called the Solomons cockatoo, is a smaller white cockatoo with a broad, triangular, sail-like crest and a bright blue eye-ring — the combination separates it from the blue-eyed cockatoo, whose crest is rounder and which lives further west. It is found across the Solomon Islands in the south-west Pacific, in lowland forest, second growth, gardens and coconut plantations. It feeds on seeds, fruit, berries, blossom and insects, and is a familiar, confiding bird around villages, often tame enough to watch at close range as it feeds. Unlike many island cockatoos it remains widespread and reasonably numerous, helped by its ability to use disturbed habitats. The IUCN Red List classifies Ducorps's cockatoo as Least Concern, though it is protected from commercial export by its CITES listing.

details.name: Palm cockatoo
details.description: The palm cockatoo (Probosciger aterrimus) is one of the world's largest parrots and looks like no other: smoky black to dark grey plumage, a huge arched black bill, a tall crest of long, spiky feathers, and a bare red cheek patch that flushes deeper crimson when the bird is excited. It lives in the rainforests and savanna woodlands of New Guinea and Australia's Cape York Peninsula. It feeds on the hard seeds of pandanus and other palms and nuts that few other birds can crack. Males are famous for drumming: a bird snaps off a stick, trims it, and beats it against a hollow dead trunk to advertise the nest hollow to females — a rare case of a bird making and using a musical instrument. Slow breeding makes it vulnerable to habitat loss. The IUCN Red List classifies it as Near Threatened, with a declining population.

details.name: Galah
details.description: The galah (Eolophus roseicapilla) is Australia's pink-and-grey cockatoo, and one of the continent's most familiar birds: rose-pink face, neck and underparts, pale grey back and wings, and a short pinkish-white crest. It lives almost everywhere in mainland Australia except the wettest forests and the driest desert core, favouring open grassland, farmland, watercourses and towns. Galahs feed on the ground in flocks on seeds, grain, roots and bulbs, and are strong, acrobatic fliers whose flocks twist and wheel in unison, flashing pink and grey. They nest in tree hollows, lining them with eucalypt leaves. Land clearing and grain farming have suited it, and numbers have grown over the last century; in Australian slang, a 'galah' is a fool, after the bird's clownish antics. The IUCN Red List classifies the galah as Least Concern.

details.name: Major Mitchell's cockatoo
details.description: Major Mitchell's cockatoo (Lophochroa leadbeateri), now often called the pink cockatoo, is the inland counterpart of the galah: soft salmon-pink underparts and face, white wings and back, and a spectacular crest banded in scarlet, yellow and white that it raises in display. It is a bird of arid and semi-arid inland Australia — mallee, mulga and cypress-pine woodland, always within reach of water. It feeds on the ground and in trees on seeds, especially native grasses and melon fruits, plus roots, nuts and insect larvae. Quieter and less gregarious than other cockatoos, it travels in pairs or family parties and needs large old hollow-bearing trees to nest. Clearing of inland woodland has fragmented its habitat across the wheat belts. The IUCN Red List classifies Major Mitchell's cockatoo as Least Concern worldwide, though numbers are falling as inland woodland is cleared.

details.name: Gang-gang cockatoo
details.description: The gang-gang cockatoo (Callocephalon fimbriatum) is a small, stocky cockatoo of cool mountain forests, slate-grey overall with fine scalloped feather edges. The male is unmistakable, with a scarlet head and a wispy, filamentous crest like a tuft of wool; the female is plainer grey with orange barring underneath, as in the photograph here. It lives in the ranges of south-eastern Australia, moving to lower coastal country in winter. Gang-gangs feed quietly in the canopy on eucalypt seeds, acacia pods, pine cones and berries such as hawthorn, cracking them in a strong bill. Their call is a strange creaking croak, often compared to a rusty gate hinge or a cork drawn from a bottle. Catastrophic bushfires have burned much of its forest home in recent years. The IUCN Red List classifies the gang-gang cockatoo as Vulnerable.

details.name: Yellow-tailed black cockatoo
details.description: The yellow-tailed black cockatoo (Zanda funerea) is a big, slow-flying forest cockatoo of eastern Australia: brownish-black plumage, a bright yellow cheek patch, and broad yellow panels in the tail that show when the tail fans open. It lives in eucalypt forest and woodland from Queensland to Victoria and Tasmania, and in pine plantations. Its speciality is extracting fat wood-boring grubs: the bird tears strips of bark and shreds dead wood with its powerful bill to reach beetle larvae, and also feeds on banksia, hakea and pine seeds. Flight is languid, with deep, slow wingbeats, and its far-carrying wailing call is one of the classic sounds of the Australian bush. It needs very old, hollow eucalypts for nesting, so it depends on mature forest. The IUCN Red List classifies it as Least Concern.

details.name: Red-tailed black cockatoo
details.description: The red-tailed black cockatoo (Calyptorhynchus banksii) is named for the panels in its tail: in males they are a plain, blazing scarlet; in females — like the bird photographed here — the tail is barred red and orange and the head and wings are speckled with yellow. It is found across northern, eastern and parts of western Australia in five subspecies, in eucalypt woodland, river corridors and savanna. It feeds mainly on seeds, of eucalypts, marri, casuarinas and acacias, husking them in a heavy bill and dropping a litter of debris beneath feeding trees. Flocks are noisy but wary, and the birds commute between feeding trees and water each morning and evening. Some southern subspecies are locally threatened by the loss of their specialised food trees. The IUCN Red List classifies the species as a whole as Least Concern.

details.name: Carnaby's black cockatoo
details.description: Carnaby's black cockatoo (Zanda latirostris) is one of two white-cheeked black cockatoos, and the way to tell it from Baudin's is the bill: Carnaby's is shorter and deeper, built for cracking hard banksia and hakea nuts, while Baudin's is longer and narrower for extracting marri seeds. The big white cheek patch shows clearly in the photograph. It lives only in south-western Western Australia, breeding in wheatbelt eucalypt woodland and moving to the coast in the non-breeding season to feed in banksia woodland and heath. It feeds on the seeds of banksias, hakeas and other proteaceous shrubs, and on insect larvae. Clearing of both its breeding woodland and its coastal feeding grounds has cut numbers steeply, and flocks now commute long distances between the two. The IUCN Red List classifies Carnaby's black cockatoo as Endangered.

details.name: Little corella
details.description: The little corella (Cacatua sanguinea) is a small, short-billed white cockatoo with a blue-grey eye-ring, a pink blush between the eye and the bill, and a lemon wash under the wings and tail that flashes in flight. It is widespread across mainland Australia and southern New Guinea, in grasslands, savanna, farmland and along watercourses. Little corellas are champion ground-feeders, digging for roots, bulbs and seeds, and in the dry season they gather in staggering flocks of thousands that swirl over waterholes at dawn. They are famously playful — sliding down roofs, swinging from wires and powerlines, and tumbling in flight — and their chattering chorus is a signature sound of the outback. Adaptable and numerous, the species thrives around farms and towns. The IUCN Red List classifies the little corella as Least Concern.

details.name: Long-billed corella
details.description: The long-billed corella (Cacatua tenuirostris) is the digging specialist among corellas: its upper bill is elongated into a slender point, an adaptation for excavating roots, bulbs and corms from the ground. It is white, with red-orange colouring around the face and a red band across the throat, and a blue-grey eye-ring. Its home is the grasslands and open woodland of south-eastern Australia, centred on Victoria and southern New South Wales. It feeds largely on the ground, using that long bill to unearth the bulbs of introduced onion grass as well as native roots and seeds, and it also strips grain. Sociable and noisy, it gathers in large flocks and shares the little corella's love of aerial play. The IUCN Red List classifies the long-billed corella as Least Concern, and its range has expanded with farmland.

details.name: Tanimbar corella
details.description: The Tanimbar corella (Cacatua goffiniana), better known to bird keepers as Goffin's cockatoo, is one of the smallest white cockatoos: white plumage, a short crest, a pale horn-coloured bill and salmon-pink lores — the patch between eye and bill that shows clearly in the photograph. It lives only on Indonesia's remote Tanimbar Islands, in forest, forest edge and cultivated land around villages. It feeds on seeds, nuts, fruit, berries and insects. In aviaries and laboratories it has become famous as one of the most inventive tool-users among birds, spontaneously making and using tools and solving multi-step puzzles, despite never using tools in the wild. Trapping for the pet trade removed large numbers from its small island range. The IUCN Red List classifies the Tanimbar corella as Near Threatened.

title: Galliformes: Pheasants, Partridges, Quail, Grouse and Other Game Birds
summary: A guide to the Galliformes — the game bird order of pheasants, partridges, quail, grouse, turkeys, guineafowl and peafowl — with 17 notable species from India and around the world, their identification, habitat and behaviour.
editorial: Galliformes are the game birds: an order of about 290 mostly heavy-bodied, ground-dwelling birds that includes the pheasants, partridges, quail, grouse, turkeys, guineafowl and peafowl — and the domestic chicken, the world's most numerous bird, descends from two of the species on this page. What defines the order is a ground-feeding build: strong legs and blunt-clawed feet for scratching in soil and leaf litter, a stout bill for seeds and invertebrates, and short, rounded wings built for explosive bursts of flight rather than long journeys. Many species are strikingly different between the sexes, with males wearing iridescent colours, crests, wattles and trains, and their chicks are precocial, leaving the nest and feeding themselves within hours of hatching. This guide focuses on identification and observation — what each bird looks like, where it lives and how it feeds — using well-established natural-history references.

details.name: Indian peafowl
details.description: The Indian peafowl is India's national bird and the original peacock of gardens and temple art. The male's iridescent blue neck and the great train — not the true tail, but elongated upper-tail coverts tipped with blue-green eye spots — are raised into a shivering fan during courtship, while the peahen is mottled brown and grey for camouflage at the ground nest. Peafowl live in scrub, open deciduous forest and farmland edges across the Indian subcontinent, feeding on the ground on seeds, shoots, insects, small reptiles and fallen fruit. They roost in trees at night, fly strongly if pressed, and the male's far-carrying, wailing call is one of the classic sounds of the Indian countryside, heard most often at dawn and before rain.

details.name: Red junglefowl
details.description: The red junglefowl is the principal wild ancestor of the domestic chicken, and a wild cock looks like a slim, athletic version of a farmyard rooster: red comb and wattles, flame-golden neck hackles, a glossy dark green-black tail, and a white patch at the tail base. It lives in forest undergrowth, bamboo and scrub across northern and north-eastern India and South-east Asia, travelling in small parties led by a dominant cock. Parties scratch through leaf litter for seeds, shoots, insects and other invertebrates, fly up into trees to roost, and the cock crows at dawn much like his domestic descendants. After the breeding season males in many populations moult into a duller eclipse plumage with shorter, darker neck feathers.

details.name: Grey junglefowl
details.description: The grey junglefowl is found only in peninsular India, in the forests, bamboo thickets and scrub of the Western and Eastern Ghats and central Indian hills. The male is unmistakable: his grey neck feathers are finely scaled and spangled with waxy yellow spots — feathers once exported for tying salmon flies — set against a dark body, chestnut wing patch and blackish tail, while the female is plain mottled brown. Grey junglefowl live in pairs or small family parties, scratching on the forest floor for seeds, shoots, termites and other insects, and roosting in trees. Studies of chicken DNA show this species also contributed genes to the domestic chicken through ancient hybridisation with the red junglefowl, including the gene for yellow skin.

details.name: Himalayan monal
details.description: The Himalayan monal, Nepal's national bird, is one of the most brilliantly coloured of all pheasants. The male seems to change colour as he turns: a metallic green crest like a bunch of tiny spoons, a coppery neck, green and purple wings and back, and a rufous-orange tail, while the female is streaked brown with a white throat, pale eye patch and short crest. Monals live on steep alpine meadows, rhododendron and oak forest in the Himalayas, mostly between about 2,700 and 4,500 metres in summer and moving lower in winter. They use their strong bills to dig for tubers, roots, shoots and insects, often leaving slopes pockmarked with probe holes, and fly downhill in fast, whistling glides.

details.name: Satyr tragopan
details.description: The satyr tragopan is a plump, secretive pheasant of the eastern Himalayas, found in moist oak, conifer and rhododendron forest with bamboo undergrowth in Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan and Arunachal Pradesh. The male is deep crimson on the neck and breast with a black head, blue facial skin, and a grey-brown back and tail densely spotted with white; displaying males inflate small blue horns and a bright bib-like lappet under the throat. The female is mottled brown and stays hidden in undergrowth. Satyr tragopans feed on the ground and in low bushes on leaves, shoots, berries, seeds and invertebrates, and are most often heard — a bleating, wailing call at dawn — rather than seen. The species is listed as Near Threatened as its forest habitat shrinks.

details.name: Cheer pheasant
details.description: The cheer pheasant is a pale grey bird boldly streaked and barred with black, with crimson skin around the eye, a short crest, and a long, broad, strongly barred tail that makes up much of its length. It lives on steep, grassy slopes scattered with scrub and pine in the western and central Himalayas, from Pakistan through Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand into Nepal, mostly on south-facing hillsides. Cheer pheasants live in pairs and family parties, digging energetically with the bill for roots, tubers, grubs and shoots, and taking seeds and berries as well. They are reluctant fliers, preferring to run uphill through grass. Habitat loss and hunting have made the species Vulnerable, and reintroduction projects have been attempted in parts of its former range.

details.name: Kalij pheasant
details.description: The kalij pheasant is a handsome forest bird of the Himalayan foothills and north-east India, ranging from Pakistan through Nepal and Bhutan to Myanmar and Thailand. The male is glossy blue-black above with fine white scaling across the lower back and rump, a floppy grey-white crest and bare red skin around the eye; the female is mottled brown with paler scaling. Kalij live in dense undergrowth of evergreen and deciduous forest, bamboo and overgrown clearings, usually in pairs or small family groups. They feed on the ground on seeds, leaves, bamboo shoots, insects and other invertebrates, scratching in leaf litter like other pheasants, and roost in trees at night. Kalij pheasants were also introduced to Hawaii, where feral birds now live in mountain forests.

details.name: Grey francolin
details.description: The grey francolin is a compact, finely barred gamebird of dry plains, scrub, thorn forest and farmland across South Asia, from Pakistan and India to Sri Lanka. Its buff-grey plumage is patterned all over with fine black barring, and the male shows a chestnut patch behind the eye and a dark border to the throat. Francolins live in pairs and small coveys, keeping close to cover and running swiftly when disturbed, bursting into low flight only at the last moment. They feed on the ground on seeds, grain, green shoots and insects, especially termites. The male's ringing, repeated call — often written ka-tee-tar, ka-tee-tar — carries far over open country at dawn and dusk, and nesting is a simple scrape on the ground under a bush.

details.name: Chukar partridge
details.description: The chukar is a sturdy, boldly patterned partridge of dry, rocky mountains from the Middle East across Central Asia to the Himalayas, where in India it lives in the hills of Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. It is sandy grey-brown above and buff below, with black-and-chestnut barred flanks, a white throat framed by a clean black band running through the eye, and coral-red bill and legs. Chukars travel in coveys over bare slopes, feeding on seeds, leaves, bulbs and insects, and they prefer to run uphill rather than fly, though they burst downhill on whirring wings when flushed. The male's chucking, chuck-chuck-chukar call gives the bird its name; it is also the national bird of Pakistan.

details.name: Japanese quail
details.description: The Japanese quail is a tiny, mottled brown ground bird of East Asian grasslands, barely 20 centimetres long, streaked and speckled for concealment in grass. Wild birds are migrants, breeding in Siberia, Mongolia, northern China and Japan and wintering further south, while the domesticated form — kept in Japan for centuries — is now raised worldwide for its eggs and meat. Males have a warm russet throat and breast, females a paler, speckled breast. Japanese quail live on the ground in grass and scrub, feeding on small seeds, green material and insects, and they almost never perch, flying low and fast only when flushed from underfoot. The male's call is a soft, liquid series of notes quite unlike the familiar 'wet-my-lips' of the common quail.

details.name: Green peafowl
details.description: The green peafowl is the Indian peafowl's larger, more elusive cousin, native to mainland South-east Asia and Java. Both sexes wear scale-like emerald and gold-green neck feathers and a straight, fan-tipped crest held bolt upright — quite unlike the Indian male's blue neck and the peahen's drab plumage — and the male's train, raised in display, is backed by coppery wing feathers. Green peafowl live in forest edges, clearings and grassland near water, feeding on the ground on seeds, fruit, insects, frogs and small snakes. They are warier than Indian peafowl and stronger fliers, roosting high in trees. Hunting and habitat loss have reduced them across much of their range, and the species is listed as Endangered.

details.name: Common pheasant
details.description: The common pheasant is the world's best-known gamebird: native across Asia from the Caucasus to China, it has been introduced to Europe, North America and elsewhere for centuries. The cock is a blaze of metallic green head, red face wattles, sometimes a white neck ring, and a copper-and-bronze body trailing an extremely long, barred tail; the hen is a modest mottled brown. Pheasants live on farmland, woodland edges, reedbeds and hedgerows, feeding on the ground on seeds, grain, berries, leaves and insects. In spring cocks defend small harems, crowing and whirring their wings from display posts. They run fast and far when disturbed, and take flight in an explosive, vertical burst before gliding to cover.

details.name: Golden pheasant
details.description: The golden pheasant of central China's mountain forests is one of the most vividly coloured birds in the world — so often kept in aviaries that many people meet it in a zoo long before knowing its wild home. The male has a silky golden crest, an orange cape barred with black that can be fanned around the head, a scarlet breast, a yellow rump and a very long, barred brown tail; the female is quietly barred brown. Golden pheasants are shy forest-floor birds, feeding in bamboo and rhododendron undergrowth on seeds, leaves, buds and invertebrates, and they fly reluctantly, preferring to run through cover. Males display by suddenly unfurling the cape to one side of the head while circling the female.

details.name: Wild turkey
details.description: The wild turkey is one of the largest galliformes: a heavy, dark bird with bronze-green iridescent plumage, a bare blue and red head, and in the tom a coarse 'beard' of modified feathers hanging from the breast. In spring display the tom fans his broad tail, swells the wattles and snood on his head, and gobbles from woodland clearings. Turkeys live in forests and oak woodland across North America, feeding on the ground on acorns and other mast, seeds, fruit and insects — poults take mostly insects. Despite their size they fly strongly to roost high in trees at night and can run at surprising speed. Domestic turkeys descend from a Mexican subspecies of this bird, taken to Europe in the 1500s.

details.name: Helmeted guineafowl
details.description: The helmeted guineafowl is a plump, unmistakable African bird: slate-grey plumage densely spotted with white, a bare blue and red head, and a bony, horn-like casque — the 'helmet' — on the crown. It is the ancestor of domestic guineafowl kept on farms worldwide. Wild flocks roam savannas, grassland and scrub across sub-Saharan Africa, travelling on foot in noisy parties that scratch and peck for insects, other invertebrates, seeds, bulbs and fallen fruit — flocks are often valued for snapping up ticks. At night they fly up to roost in trees. Their harsh, rattling calls carry over the savanna, and when danger threatens the whole flock streams away on foot before taking wing.

details.name: Western capercaillie
details.description: The western capercaillie is the largest grouse in the world, a massive bird of old conifer forests across northern Europe and Siberia. The cock is black with a green-sheened breast, a broad fan-shaped tail, a scarlet patch above the eye and a white spot on the wing, and he weighs several times more than the barred brown hen. In spring, males gather at traditional display grounds called leks, where they produce an extraordinary song of clicks and pops ending in a cork-from-bottle note, tails fanned and heads raised. Capercaillie feed on the ground and in trees: bilberries, shoots and insects in summer, and mostly pine needles through the winter, which their gut is specially adapted to digest.

details.name: Greater sage-grouse
details.description: The greater sage-grouse is a large, mottled brown grouse of North America's sagebrush plains, completely dependent on that one shrub: it shelters in sagebrush, nests under it, and eats its leaves, especially through winter, alongside summer flowers and insects. The male is famous for his spring display at communal leks, where he fans a crown of spiky tail feathers, puffs out a great white chest ruff and inflates two yellow air sacs on the neck to make deep popping sounds that carry across the plain at dawn. Females are smaller and plainer, relying on camouflage. Because sagebrush country has been widely cleared and fragmented, the species has declined over much of its range and is listed as Near Threatened.

title: Songbirds: Nightingales, Thrushes, Robins and the Great Singers of Gardens, Woods and Fields
summary: A guide to 17 birds celebrated for their song — nightingale, blackbird, song thrush, robins, skylark, canary, goldfinch, cardinal, mockingbird, meadowlark, wren, magpie-robin, shama, bulbul, oriole and the koel — with identification, range and the song each one is famous for.
editorial: True songbirds are the oscines, the large songbird suborder of the passerines (perching birds), whose specialised voice box — the syrinx — lets them learn and perform complex songs. Nearly every bird in this guide is an oscine; the one famous exception, the Asian koel, is a cuckoo, and its entry says so plainly. This guide is about natural song — the dawn chorus, territorial singing and birdsong as identification — which is a different subject from the mimicry covered in our Talking Birds guide. Statements follow standard field-guide and reference consensus.

details.name: Common nightingale
details.description: The common nightingale is a small, plain brown bird — warm russet above, paler below, with a rufous tail — that is far more often heard than seen, singing from deep inside thickets, coppices and dense scrub across Europe and south-western Asia, and wintering in sub-Saharan Africa. Its song is the most celebrated in birdsong: a rich, varied outpouring of whistles, trills, crescendos and deep throbbing notes, delivered by day and famously through the night in spring, when unpaired males sing to attract migrants arriving in the dark. Nightingales skulk low in cover, hopping on the ground to pick up insects, spiders and other invertebrates, and berries in autumn. The singer is so hidden that the species' name in several languages simply means 'night singer'.

details.name: Eurasian blackbird
details.description: The Eurasian blackbird is one of Europe and Asia's most familiar birds: the male is glossy black all over with a bright orange-yellow bill and eye-ring, while the female is sooty brown with a duller bill. Its song — a relaxed, fluting warble of clear, mellow phrases, usually delivered from a rooftop, tree or chimney at dawn and dusk — is ranked by many listeners alongside the nightingale's, though the blackbird sings in daylight and at a leisurely pace, often ending a phrase with a quiet chuckle. Blackbirds inhabit woods, parks and gardens across Europe and much of Asia and have been introduced to Australia and New Zealand. They feed on the ground, tossing leaf litter aside for earthworms and insects, and take berries and fallen fruit in autumn and winter.

details.name: Song thrush
details.description: The song thrush is a neat, warm-brown thrush with bold dark spots on a creamy-white breast, found in woods, parks and gardens across Europe and western Asia and introduced to New Zealand and Australia. It is the great repeater of the bird world: from a high treetop perch it delivers loud, clear phrases of whistles and trills, repeating each motif two to four times before moving to the next, so its song sounds deliberate and almost musical in structure. Song thrushes feed on the ground on earthworms, insects and berries, and are famous for smashing snail shells against a favourite stone 'anvil' to reach the soft body inside. Northern populations migrate south and west in winter, while birds in milder western areas stay resident all year.

details.name: European robin
details.description: The European robin is a plump little bird with an orange-red face and breast, olive-brown upperparts and a pale belly, found across Europe to western Siberia and North Africa in woods, hedgerows and gardens, where it often follows gardeners for turned-up worms. Unusually among songbirds, both sexes hold territories and sing through autumn and winter as well as spring, so the robin's wistful, rippling song — clear phrases with a slightly melancholy fall — can be heard on the darkest December days, sometimes under streetlights at night. Robins are fiercely territorial and quick to challenge rivals, yet famously tame around people. They feed on insects, spiders, worms and seeds, taking mealworms and crumbs readily from bird tables in hard weather.

details.name: Eurasian skylark
details.description: The Eurasian skylark is a streaky brown bird of open country — farmland, grassland, moor and marsh across Europe and Asia — with a small crest it can raise on its head and white outer tail feathers that flash as it flies. It is celebrated for its song flight: the male climbs almost vertically, singing an unbroken, pouring stream of trills and warbles for minutes at a time while hovering high overhead, then parachutes silently down to the ground, where the nest is a grass cup hidden among low vegetation. Skylarks walk on the ground feeding on seeds, leaves and insects, and in winter they gather in flocks on stubble fields. Sadly, skylark numbers have fallen sharply across much of western Europe as farming has intensified.

details.name: Atlantic canary
details.description: The Atlantic canary is the wild original of the familiar cage bird: a small, yellow-green finch, streaked brown above, that lives only in Macaronesia — the Canary Islands (which take their name from the bird, via the Latin for dogs on the islands), Madeira and the Azores. Wild males are much less uniformly yellow than domestic canaries, with grey-green backs and streaked flanks. From a prominent perch the male pours out a sweet, liquid song of trills and twitters through much of the year, and it was this song, together with the plumage, that led islanders to export the birds to Europe from the fifteenth century, founding the cage-bird trade. In the wild, canaries live in orchards, gardens, vineyards and open woodland, feeding mainly on small seeds and buds in sociable flocks.

details.name: European goldfinch
details.description: The European goldfinch is one of Europe's most colourful finches: a crimson face mask, black-and-white head pattern, warm buff body and black wings split by a broad golden-yellow bar that flashes in its bounding flight. It ranges across Europe, North Africa and western and central Asia, and has been introduced to Australia, New Zealand and parts of the Americas. Its song is a delicate, tinkling twitter built around a distinctive repeated 'tickelit' call, often delivered from a treetop or while swaying on a seed head. Goldfinches specialise in tiny seeds that heavier birds cannot reach: their fine bills extract seeds from thistles, teasels and dandelions while the bird hangs acrobatically, and flocks — charmingly called charms — wander farmland and waste ground in winter.

details.name: Northern cardinal
details.description: The northern cardinal is the crested, scarlet songster of North American gardens, woodland edges and thickets from southern Canada through the eastern and central United States to Mexico. The male is brilliant red with a black mask and a stout orange-red bill for cracking seeds; the female is warm olive-buff with red tints in the wings, tail and crest — and, unusually among songbirds, she sings too, sometimes duetting with her mate from the nest. The cardinal's song is a series of loud, clear, down-slurred whistles — 'cheer, cheer, cheer' and 'birdy, birdy, birdy' — sung through much of the year from a high perch. Cardinals do not migrate; pairs hold their territory year-round, which is why the red male against winter snow has become an iconic image.

details.name: Northern mockingbird
details.description: The northern mockingbird is a slim, grey songbird of North American gardens, parks and open country, with a long tail, pale wing bars and white wing patches that flash conspicuously when it flies or performs its wing-flashing display. Its scientific name, Mimus polyglottos — 'many-tongued mimic' — is earned: the male strings together long sequences of borrowed songs and sounds, each repeated several times before switching, learning phrases from dozens of other species and even mechanical noises, and sings for hours, sometimes through moonlit nights. Mockingbirds are bold defenders of their territory, diving at cats, crows and people who come too close to the nest. They feed on insects in summer and berries in winter, and are resident year-round across most of their range.

details.name: Western meadowlark
details.description: The western meadowlark is a stocky, streaked-brown bird of North American grasslands, instantly recognised in breeding dress by its bright yellow underparts crossed by a bold black V on the breast. From a fence post or bush top the male delivers one of the most loved sounds of the prairies: a rich, flute-like song of clear whistles that ripple and gurgle downhill, quite unlike the harsh rattle of its near-identical twin, the eastern meadowlark — the two are best separated by voice. Meadowlarks walk on the ground probing for insects such as grasshoppers and beetles, and in winter they also take seeds and grain. The nest is a domed cup of grass hidden on the ground. Northern birds move south in winter as frozen ground cuts off their food.

details.name: Eurasian wren
details.description: The Eurasian wren is one of Europe's smallest birds — a tiny, round, warm-brown bird with fine barring, a short tail it cocks jauntily upright, and a loud voice wildly out of proportion to its size. Its song is an explosive, rapid-fire burst of trills and warbles, delivered from a low perch with the whole body trembling; for its weight it is among the loudest singers in the bird world. Wrens creep mouse-like through dense undergrowth, rock piles, banks and garden shrubbery across Europe and Asia (close relatives range into North America), hunting spiders and small insects in crevices. The male builds several domed nests in cavities and lets a female choose one. Harsh winters with prolonged snow can kill huge numbers, but populations bounce back quickly.

details.name: Oriental magpie-robin
details.description: The oriental magpie-robin is a neat black-and-white songbird of gardens, open woodland and cultivation across South and South East Asia, from India and Sri Lanka to southern China and Indonesia. The male is glossy black above with a white belly, white shoulder patch and long black-and-white tail, which it constantly cocks and fans as it hops on lawns and low perches; the female is the same pattern in slaty grey. At dawn the male takes a high, exposed perch and delivers a clear, melodious song of varied whistles and phrases, often borrowing motifs from other birds — it is one of India's best-loved singers, known as the dayal, and was long kept as a cage and fighting bird. It feeds on the ground on insects, worms and other small creatures.

details.name: Indian robin
details.description: The Indian robin is a dashing little songbird of dry, open country across the Indian subcontinent — scrub, stony ground, gardens, ruins and village edges. The male of the northern form is glossy black with a white shoulder patch and a rich chestnut patch under the tail, which flashes each time the bird cocks its tail upright — a constant, perky habit; southern males are browner-backed, and females everywhere are grey-brown with the same chestnut vent. From a rock, post or rooftop the male sings a cheery, varied warbling song, strongest in the breeding season, and pairs are familiar, confiding birds around habitation. Indian robins feed on the ground, running and hopping after insects and spiders, and nest in holes in walls, banks and stone heaps.

details.name: White-rumped shama
details.description: The white-rumped shama is widely rated among the finest songbirds on Earth. The male is glossy black above with a deep chestnut belly, a striking white rump and lower back, and an exceptionally long black-and-white graduated tail; the female is a greyer, shorter-tailed version. In the lowland forests and bamboo thickets of South and South East Asia, from India to Indonesia, the male sings at dawn and through the day from a shaded perch — a powerful, rich, endlessly varied performance of fluty whistles, trills and expert mimicry of other birds. That voice made it one of Asia's most prized cage birds, and trapping has thinned wild populations in places. In the wild it hops on the forest floor and low branches, taking insects and other small invertebrates.

details.name: Red-whiskered bulbul
details.description: The red-whiskered bulbul is a jaunty, crest-headed songbird of gardens, scrub and open forest across tropical Asia, from India and southern China through South East Asia, and it has established introduced populations in places as far apart as Florida, Mauritius and Australia. It is easily told by its tall black crest, white cheek patch, the small crimson 'whisker' spot below the eye and a red patch under the tail. Its song is a bright, musical series of clear notes — often rendered 'pleased-to-meet-you' — delivered from exposed perches, and pairs keep up a lively chattering contact. Gregarious outside the breeding season, red-whiskered bulbuls feed on fruit, berries, nectar and insects, and play a useful role spreading the seeds of the fruit they eat.

details.name: Indian golden oriole
details.description: The Indian golden oriole is a bird of the treetops across the Indian subcontinent, breeding in open woodland, groves and large gardens and moving south within the subcontinent in winter. The adult male is unmistakable — brilliant golden yellow with black wings, black tail markings and a strong pinkish-red bill; the female is duller yellow-green with streaked underparts and is easily overlooked among leaves. Despite the colouring, orioles are shy canopy birds usually located by their song: a rich, fluting, liquid whistle, often written 'peelo' or 'wee-lo', rising and falling through the branches. They feed high in the canopy on fruit such as figs and berries, and on insects including hairy caterpillars that few birds will touch, and build a neat hammock-like cup nest slung in a forked branch.

details.name: Asian koel
details.description: The Asian koel is included with a plain taxonomic note: it is not a true songbird at all, but a cuckoo — yet few sounds define an Indian summer like its voice, the insistent, rising 'ku-oo, ku-oo' that climbs in pitch and urgency through the breeding season, sung mainly by the male. The male is glossy blue-black with striking crimson eyes; the female is brown, heavily speckled and barred with white — so different she was once thought a separate species. Koels range across South and South East Asia to northern Australia, in gardens, groves and open woodland. Like many cuckoos the koel is a brood parasite, laying its eggs in the nests of crows and other hosts, and unusually among cuckoos the adults feed mainly on fruit, especially figs.

title: Scariest Animals in the World: The Truly Dangerous — and the Ones That Only Look It
summary: Sixteen of the world's most frightening animals — crocodiles, sharks, jellyfish, spiders and deep-sea oddities — with an honest split between the ones that are genuinely dangerous to people and the ones whose terrifying looks hide a harmless nature.
editorial: Scary is not the same as dangerous. This guide mixes animals that really can kill — a saltwater crocodile, a box jellyfish, a funnel-web spider — with animals that merely look the part, like the aye-aye and the goblin shark. Each entry states the real level of risk plainly, without exaggeration: what the animal can do, how encounters actually happen, and how they are avoided. No death tolls or attack statistics are quoted, because for most of these animals the commonly repeated figures cannot be traced to a reliable source.

details.name: Saltwater crocodile
details.description: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile: males commonly reach four to five metres, and exceptional individuals exceed six. Broad-snouted and heavily armoured, it lives in estuaries, rivers, mangrove swamps and coastal waters from India's east coast — including the Sundarbans, where the photograph above was taken — through South-East Asia to northern Australia and the western Pacific. It hunts by patience, waiting submerged at the water's edge with only eyes and nostrils showing, then lunging at fish, birds, pigs, deer and even buffalo. The real risk is exactly what it looks like: this is a big territorial predator, and people are occasionally taken, usually at the water's edge, in small boats or after dark. Heed warning signs and never swim in crocodile waterways.

details.name: Hippopotamus
details.description: The common hippopotamus spends its days half-submerged in the rivers and lakes of sub-Saharan Africa and comes ashore after dark to graze. Behind the almost comic barrel body sits an enormous mouth that opens nearly 180 degrees, armed with tusk-like canine teeth that can reach about half a metre and stay sharp by grinding against each other. Hippos are strict vegetarians, but bulls are fiercely territorial in the water and mothers defend calves aggressively, and a hippo on land can charge faster than a person can run over a short distance. The real risk arises when a boat, canoe or walker gets between a hippo and deep water, or between a mother and her calf. Give hippos a very wide berth, especially at dawn and dusk.

details.name: Great white shark
details.description: The great white is the world's largest predatory shark, growing to about six metres, grey above and white below so that it is camouflaged from both above and below. It patrols temperate coasts worldwide — South Africa, Australia, California, Mexico and the Mediterranean among them — and hunts seals and sea lions by rocketing up from deep water. The fear it inspires is out of proportion to the facts, but it is not baseless: great whites account for more recorded unprovoked bites on people than any other shark species, most of them on surfers and swimmers. Even so, bites are rare, and most appear to be a single investigative bite after which the shark moves on — people are not its prey. The species is vulnerable and protected in many countries.

details.name: Australian box jellyfish
details.description: Chironex fleckeri, the Australian box jellyfish or sea wasp, is a pale, transparent cube of a jellyfish with up to sixty tentacles trailing as far as three metres from a bell about the size of a basketball. It drifts through the tropical shallows of northern Australia and the wider Indo-Pacific, hunting small fish and prawns, and it is considered one of the most venomous animals on Earth: a bad sting floods the skin with venom that can affect the heart, and severe stings have killed within minutes. The real risk is seasonal and manageable — stings happen almost entirely in the warmer 'stinger season', roughly October to May, when swimmers should use stinger-net enclosures. Vinegar, kept at tropical Australian beaches, is the recommended first aid because it stops unfired stinging cells from discharging.

details.name: Sydney funnel-web spider
details.description: The Sydney funnel-web spider is a stocky, glossy-black spider up to about five centimetres long, with a bulky body, powerful fangs and a famously defensive temper when disturbed — it rears up and shows its fangs rather than fleeing. It lives in silk-lined burrows under rocks, logs and gardens within roughly a hundred kilometres of Sydney, and in summer and autumn the males wander at night, sometimes ending up in swimming pools, shoes and houses. Its venom contains a compound called atraxotoxin that is unusually dangerous to primates, including people. The honest picture, though, is reassuring: bites are uncommon, an antivenom has been available since 1981, and no confirmed deaths have been recorded since its introduction. A firm pressure-immobilisation bandage is the correct first aid.

details.name: Reef stonefish
details.description: The reef stonefish is generally regarded as the most venomous fish in the world, and it looks like a piece of the reef itself — a warty, encrusted, algae-flecked lump that sits utterly still on sand and rubble in the shallow waters of the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea. Along its back stands a row of thirteen spines, each linked to a venom gland and wrapped in a sheath that peels back when something presses down on it. The stonefish does not attack: the real risk is stepping on one while wading barefoot, which drives the spines into the foot and causes intense, sometimes life-threatening envenomation. Wearing reef shoes or sturdy sandals in rocky shallows is simple, effective protection, and hot-water first aid and antivenom exist for stings.

details.name: Blue-ringed octopus
details.description: Blue-ringed octopuses are tiny — the southern species pictured here is small enough to sit in the palm of a hand — and normally a dull yellowish-brown. Disturb one, though, and it flashes brilliant iridescent blue rings and spots across its body: a warning worth obeying. These octopuses live in tide pools and shallow reefs around Australia and the western Pacific, sheltering in shells and crevices and hunting small crabs and shrimp. They carry tetrodotoxin, the same potent nerve toxin found in pufferfish, in their saliva. The bite itself is often barely felt, and there is no antivenom; treatment means supporting breathing until the toxin wears off. Bites are rare and in practice almost always follow somebody picking the animal up — admire it, photograph it, and leave it exactly where it is.

details.name: Cape buffalo
details.description: The Cape buffalo is a massive, dark bovid of sub-Saharan savannas and wetlands, its horns fused into a heavy shield — the boss — across the forehead. Herds can number in the hundreds, grazing and wallowing by day, and old bulls, which can approach 900 kilograms, often drift apart into small bachelor groups. Buffalo are not predators, but hunters and rangers have long respected them as among Africa's most dangerous animals, and the reputation has a basis: a buffalo that is wounded, cornered or surprised at close range may charge with little warning, and a herd will sometimes turn and mob a lion that has taken a calf. Unprovoked attacks on people are uncommon; the sensible rule on foot in buffalo country is distance, a clear escape route, and never approaching a lone bull closely.

details.name: Southern cassowary
details.description: The southern cassowary is a tall, flightless bird of the rainforests of north-eastern Queensland and New Guinea, standing up to about 1.8 metres, with glossy black feathers, a bare blue neck with red wattles, and a tall helmet-like casque whose purpose is still debated. It is a shy fruit-eater that plants the rainforest as it goes, swallowing fruit whole and dispersing the seeds across the forest floor. The danger is in its feet: the inner toe of each foot carries a straight, dagger-like claw up to about twelve centimetres long, and a cornered cassowary — or a male guarding chicks — can leap and kick with both feet at once. Attacks are rare and two fatal incidents are on record, in 1926 and 2019, the second involving a captive bird. Never feed or crowd one.

details.name: Spotted hyena
details.description: The spotted hyena is a powerful, sloping-backed predator of sub-Saharan Africa, living in clans that can number dozens and filling the night with whoops, giggles and the famous 'laugh'. Its head and neck are built around one of the strongest bites among land mammals, able to crack open large bones that lions leave behind and digest almost every part of a carcass. Research over the past half-century has rewritten its image: spotted hyenas hunt much of what they eat rather than merely scavenging, and they are social, intelligent animals with a strict clan hierarchy. The real risk to people is low — hyenas generally keep away from us — but they are large wild predators: incidents do occur where they are fed, habituated, or find people sleeping in the open, and livestock owners across Africa live with regular conflict.

details.name: Titan triggerfish
details.description: The titan triggerfish is the largest of the triggerfishes, reaching about 75 centimetres, with a deep, armour-plated body, small beak-like teeth strong enough to crush sea urchins and coral, and an unsettling habit of watching divers with one swivelling eye. It lives on lagoons and outer reefs across the Indo-Pacific. For most of the year it minds its own business, but in the breeding season a female builds a crater nest in the sand and guards a cone-shaped territory that widens towards the surface directly above it. A diver who swims up into that cone may be charged and bitten, and the teeth can draw blood even through a wetsuit. The correct escape, as dive briefings across the tropics repeat, is to fin away horizontally at the same depth — never straight up.

details.name: Coconut crab
details.description: The coconut crab is the largest land-living arthropod in the world: a hermit crab that outgrows shells as a juvenile and spends its adult life on the forest floor of islands scattered across the Indian and Pacific Oceans, spanning up to about a metre from leg to leg. It climbs palms, feeds on fallen fruit, carrion and famously on coconuts, which it husks and cracks with its huge left claw. That claw is genuinely formidable — a 2016 study measured its pinch at up to about 3,300 newtons, a force in the same league as the bites of large predators. Yet the crab itself is slow, shy and entirely non-aggressive: the only realistic injury is a severe pinch to fingers that probe, grab or tease it. It is also vulnerable to over-collection and rated Vulnerable by the IUCN.

details.name: Goliath birdeater
details.description: The Goliath birdeater of the rainforest floor in northern South America is among the heaviest spiders in the world, with a leg span that can approach 28 centimetres and a body the size of a small fist. Its alarming name comes from an eighteenth-century engraving showing one eating a hummingbird; in reality it mostly takes earthworms, frogs, large insects and the occasional small rodent, subduing them with fangs up to a few centimetres long. For all that bulk, the reality does not match the nightmare. Its venom is comparatively mild for people — often compared with a wasp sting — and it seldom bites. Its first line of defence is to kick a cloud of barbed, urticating hairs from its abdomen, which irritate skin and eyes and are best simply kept away from.

details.name: Japanese spider crab
details.description: Stilt-walking across the deep seabed around Japan, the Japanese spider crab is the largest arthropod alive measured by span: up to about 3.7 metres from claw tip to claw tip, carried on ten spindly legs around a knobbly body only about forty centimetres across. It lives at depths of roughly 150 to 600 metres, scavenging dead animals and shelly invertebrates from the sediment, and it is thought to live for many decades. Face to face in an aquarium it looks like a creature from a horror film, all spikes and improbable proportions. In truth it is slow, gentle and completely harmless to people: no venom, no aggression, and claws suited to picking at carrion rather than fighting. It is occasionally caught by trawlers and prized as food in Japan — the danger runs entirely in the other direction.

details.name: Goblin shark
details.description: The goblin shark looks like a mistake from the deep past: a soft, flabby, pinkish-grey shark with a long, flattened blade for a snout and a set of jaws that, when prey is close, catapult forward out of its mouth to snap it up. It lives in deep water — generally between about 100 and 1,300 metres down — over continental slopes worldwide, and is most often recorded off Japan, where it was first described. The snout is covered in sensors that detect the faint electric fields of fish and squid in total darkness. Because it almost never comes near the surface, nearly everything known about it comes from specimens hauled up accidentally in deep nets and trawls. To people it is no danger at all: a living fossil we are lucky to glimpse, not a threat to fear.

details.name: Aye-aye
details.description: The aye-aye is a nocturnal lemur found only in Madagascar, and it looks assembled from spare parts: huge membranous ears, staring orange eyes, ever-growing front teeth like a rodent's, and one impossibly thin, ball-jointed middle finger on each hand. It uses that finger in a technique found in no other primate — tapping rapidly on dead wood, listening for hollow spaces where grubs tunnel, gnawing a hole, then hooking the insect out with the skeletal finger. None of this apparatus is aimed at us: the aye-aye eats insects, fruit and nectar, has no venom and no interest in people. The tragedy of its frightening face is that in parts of Madagascar it is traditionally considered an omen of death and is killed on sight — persecution that, along with forest loss, has left the species Endangered.
